instructions:
GENERATE LESSONS WITH DURABLE CHECKPOINTS

This file contains the whole tree and the shared teaching rules once. tree.nodes provides each node's context; queue is the recommended order, and completed lists lessons already available. Generate only queue nodes. Never change the tree's ids, labels, scopes, prerequisites, or language. Do not include personal learning progress.

For each node, use label as its topic and explanation as its learning goal and boundary. Its requires point to earlier lessons: use those nodes' exact labels and scopes as already-taught background. Do not assume independent sibling topics. Nodes requiring this one are future material: do not teach them or mention their names. Do not repeat the design rules for each node.

COMMIT EACH LESSON BEFORE STARTING ANOTHER
Return one independent JSON object per line (JSONL), with no enclosing array, required header, or global closing marker. Each record uses exactly format="learning-tree-lesson/v1", treeKey=the treeKey in this file, id=the node id, and content=the entire finished lesson text. Use a JSON serializer when tools are available; escape newlines as \n, quotes as \" and every literal backslash in lesson text as \\. Decoded content must preserve LaTeX and every lesson marker. Never emit drafts or incomplete content records. Review the lesson, publish or save its record, then start the next one. Do not repeat records already completed in this chat or listed in completed.

WITHOUT FILE TOOLS: publish each finished record immediately in the chat. You may use a separate jsonl code fence for each record; each record inside must occupy one physical line. The maximum per reply is as many as safely fit. Use fewer when needed to finish cleanly. Do not reduce lesson quality or scope to fit more nodes. When told Continue, proceed to the next pending node under these same rules without asking for the prompt again. If cut off, earlier complete records remain importable; only the unfinished record is lost. Text never published or saved cannot be recovered.

WITH FILE TOOLS: create a downloadable .jsonl journal and expose it after the first complete record. Append and save each complete record before continuing; use atomic writes or a complete-line append and flush when available. Do not save only at the end. Continue through queue while able; the chat reply maximum does not limit tool-based work. Preserve earlier checkpoints if a later lesson fails. For a known usage limit, reserve room to expose the last saved checkpoint. You may additionally produce a usable tree JSON by inserting each content into its tree node and saving atomically after each lesson; preserve structure, and never replace the journal with one giant rewrite. JSONL records are the interruption fallback.

IF SUBAGENTS ARE AVAILABLE: use a small wave of independent nodes whose prerequisites are already in completed or committed by the coordinator. Share the teaching rules once per worker and only the relevant node context. A single coordinator validates and commits each result as soon as it arrives. Do not have every worker rewrite the whole tree or write to one shared file. Do not start descendants until their prerequisites are committed. Preserve logical learning order and prioritize a usable path. Without subagents, work sequentially using the identical format.

SHARED RULES FOR EACH DECODED content
The plain-text restrictions below apply to lesson content, not its JSONL envelope. The topic and CONTEXT vary by node; every other teaching rule stays the same.

RESUME BACKUPS: when completed is nonempty, this work file deliberately omits those lessons’ text. A JSON built only from this packet does not contain all earlier lessons. Keep the journal of new records to merge into the original tree; export the complete backup from the app after importing.

You are producing a plain-text learning document (.txt) for the topic: the current node’s label

Write this lesson text as content in one completed record under the checkpoint protocol above. Do not create an individual .txt file.

Write for an average student encountering this node's material for the first time, with the background described in CONTEXT. The lesson should help them make sense of the idea and use it at the intended level. Mathematical correctness and readable markup are necessary, but so are motivation, accessible examples, and a manageable sequence. Plan the lesson before drafting; let its length follow the learning goal.

HOW MANY QUESTIONS, AND HOW EACH ONE IS MARKED

The number of main questions should be however many it actually takes to verify that every main idea in this document has landed — and landed as something the reader can use, not just something they can recognize or recite. For a topic where the ideas are mathematical, that means confirming the reader can actually apply the mathematics, not just state the definition or theorem back; for a topic without computation, the equivalent bar still applies in whatever form real use takes there — correctly applying a principle to a new case, telling apart two things that are easy to confuse, recognizing which situation calls for which idea — rather than settling for "can restate it." Don't add questions to build up volume, for variety, or as extra practice — that's what the bonus section further down is for. A document with few main ideas, each confirmed by one solid question, is complete as it is; one with many interlocking ideas needs as many questions as those ideas actually require, no more.

Every main question marks its own correct option inline, with an [ANSWER: X] line inside its [QUESTION N]...[/QUESTION] block — see OUTPUT FORMAT below. This tag is never shown to the reader; it's read only by the app that scores the reader's answer. Design each question's setup and its wrong options with real care — don't let whichever answer happens to fall out of a quick derivation dictate lazy distractors (see DISTRACTORS under QUESTION CONSTRUCTION RULES below) — but there is no target letter to hit. Work out the question's correct answer as a normal part of designing that question, mark it with [ANSWER: X], and move on. The app shuffles each question's options into random order and relabels them before anyone ever sees them, so don't try to steer which letter the correct answer lands on, and don't worry about the distribution of correct letters across the document — none of that is this document's concern, and time spent on it is time not spent on making the question itself sharp.

PLAN FIRST

- Read CONTEXT as a learning goal and scope boundary. Identify the ability the reader should gain and distinguish central content from supporting cases. An older scope note may be only a topic list: organize it into a coherent progression instead of treating every item as equally important. Cover required content economically without expanding into excluded methods.
- Choose a meaningful question that gives the central idea a purpose within this scope. Motivation can be a concrete interpretive problem; it need not require techniques or later applications the reader has not learned.
- Choose an accessible example that can carry the first explanation. Check all its background knowledge against CONTEXT. Prefer a simple case that exposes the idea over an impressive case that adds unfamiliar machinery.
- Plan the order in which meaning, notation, general statements, worked use, and important contrasts become understandable. Identify likely misconceptions, including ones your own wording or pictures could create.
- Decide what justification the intended level needs. Distinguish an illustration or estimate from a general guarantee, but do not turn an informal introduction into a proof lesson. Make abstract phrases concrete before asking the reader to reason with them.
- Plan questions that first check understanding and then transfer it to a fresh case. Work out each answer and its distractors before committing to the setup.
- For visual objects, plan graphs where they first help the reader understand the object. Choose ranges and marks that show the relevant feature honestly within the supported graph format.



OUTPUT FORMAT (follow exactly — a parser will read this file)

This is a plain .txt file. Rules:
- No markdown: no **, no ##, no backticks, no bullet points using *, no _italics_ — including using ** to fake bold for a vector symbol (e.g. **S**); that's KaTeX's job (\mathbf{}), not markdown's, see the Math rule below
- No HTML, no code blocks, no widgets, and no interactive elements of any kind — the one exception is the slider line a graph block can carry (see Graphs below), which is part of the graph format, not HTML
- Prose only — use plain paragraphs and the section/question/table/timeline/graph markers below

Section headers:
=== SECTION N: TITLE ===

The very first line of the document must be "=== SECTION 1: TITLE ===" — nothing precedes it. No title line, no opening sentence, no framing paragraph sits above the first section header; start the lesson at that marker so its structure is clear.

Questions must use this format exactly:

[QUESTION N]
[ANSWER: X]
Question text here, with \( LaTeX \) as needed.

(A) first option
(B) second option
(C) third option
(D) fourth option
(E) fifth option
[/QUESTION]

Replace X with whichever letter is actually correct, as (A)-(E) are written above. This works exactly like the [ANSWER: X] tag in the [BONUS] format further down — hidden from the reader, read only by the app, and not something to think about when deciding where to place the correct option among (A)-(E); place it wherever it naturally falls as you write the options, in any order you like. Nothing anywhere else in the document — before this block, after it, or much later — may explain, defend, or hint at why the correct option is correct or a wrong option is wrong. [ANSWER: X] is the only place that answer lives.

Four tools are available. Math, tables and timelines are for material that has something to typeset, compare, or put in order: don't force KaTeX onto a topic without math, or a table or timeline onto material with no tabular or chronological structure. Graphs are different: they are the default, not an extra. Whenever a section's central object has a shape — a function, a curve, a surface, a field, a relationship between two quantities, a configuration of points and lines in a plane — draw it, at the point where that section first works with it, so the reader sees the object while the prose is analyzing it. Prose alone asks the reader to hold in their head a picture that a graph hands over for free. Skip a graph only when the section has nothing visual to show: purely symbolic manipulation, a definition with no geometric content, non-quantitative material. A document on a topic with geometry in it that comes out with no graph at all has a gap, and the final review below checks for it.

- Math: inline with \( ... \), display with \[ ... \]. Skip entirely for a topic with nothing to typeset. This applies uniformly — there is no such thing as a mathematical symbol too minor or too casual to wrap. A single variable name, a subscript, a dot or cross product, a vector mentioned in passing mid-sentence: if it's math, it goes in \( \), with exactly the same treatment as a formula on its own display line. Don't let a symbol's position — sitting inside a flowing sentence versus standing alone — decide whether it gets KaTeX; a parser reading this file can't tell "casual mention" from "official equation," and treating them differently is what produces a document that's formatted one way in its displayed equations and drifts into bare ASCII (r_u, F · n) the moment the same math shows up in prose. Bold or vector notation is no exception to the no-markdown rule either — never fake it with ** (e.g. **S** for a bold vector); use the real KaTeX command (\mathbf{}) inside \( \) instead.
- Tables, for anything genuinely tabular — a comparison across several things along the same dimensions, a small reference of values, anything a reader would otherwise have to hold in their head across several sentences:
[TABLE]
Header A | Header B | Header C
Row 1 col A | Row 1 col B | Row 1 col C
Row 2 col A | Row 2 col B | Row 2 col C
[/TABLE]
  First line is the header row; every line is cells separated by " | " — always with a single space on each side, exactly as in the example above. That spacing is what a column divider actually looks like; a bare "|" with no space around it (an absolute value bar, a norm, a set-builder pipe, sitting inside a cell's own math) is read as content, not a divider, so you don't need to avoid literal pipes in table-cell math. Still, prefer \lvert ... \rvert over bare | ... | for absolute value inside a table cell — it typesets with better spacing — and never use \| for a single absolute-value bar; that's a different symbol (‖, a norm). Keep cells short — this renders as a real table, not a wall of prose crammed into cells.
- Timelines, for a genuine chronology or ordered progression — a sequence of dated events, stages, or steps where the ordering itself is part of what's being taught:
[TIMELINE]
Marker 1 | What happened or what this stage is
Marker 2 | What happened or what this stage is
[/TIMELINE]
  The marker is usually a date or year but can be any short label — a stage name, "Step 1," an era — whatever the sequence is actually ordered by. One line per point on the timeline, marker and description separated by " | " (spaced, same convention as TABLE above, for the same reason — it's what tells a real divider apart from a bare pipe that happens to sit inside the marker or description's own math).
- Graphs, for a function, curve, surface, field, or set of points and lines that is worth seeing rather than just describing — see the paragraph above for when a graph is expected, and the notes after the four types for how to make one earn its place. There are four types:

  function2d — one or more y = f(x) curves on the same axes:
[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: what this graph shows
xlabel: x
ylabel: y
xrange: -5, 5
trace: x^2 - 3*x | label: f(x)
trace: 2*x - 3 | label: f'(x)
[/GRAPH]

  parametric2d — one or more curves traced out by (x(t), y(t)):
[GRAPH]
type: parametric2d
title: what this graph shows
xlabel: x
ylabel: y
trange: 0, 6.283
trace: cos(t), sin(t) | label: unit circle
[/GRAPH]

  surface3d — a single surface z = f(x, y):
[GRAPH]
type: surface3d
title: what this graph shows
xlabel: x
ylabel: y
zlabel: z
xrange: -3, 3
yrange: -3, 3
z: x^2 - y^2
[/GRAPH]

  vectorfield2d — a single vector field, given by its two components as functions of x and y:
[GRAPH]
type: vectorfield2d
title: what this graph shows
xlabel: x
ylabel: y
xrange: -3, 3
yrange: -3, 3
u: -y
v: x
[/GRAPH]

  function2d, parametric2d and vectorfield2d graphs can also carry marked points, drawn segments, and sliders: extra lines in the same block, all optional, repeatable, and not available for surface3d. Optional too is "aspect: equal" (function2d), which gives both axes the same unit length — use it whenever the true shape or an angle matters; parametric2d and vectorfield2d already do this on their own.

point: x, y | label: caption | color: optional | offset: dx, dy
segment: x1, y1, x2, y2 | label: caption | color: optional | dashed: true
slider: name | range: min, max | init: value | step: size

  A point marks one specific location the prose works with (a given data point, an intercept, a place of interest). A segment connects two locations (a distance, a change along each axis, a side of a figure, a stretch between two points). Their coordinates are plain expressions in the same calculator notation as the traces. A slider adds a draggable control under the plot, and any trace, point, or segment expression that uses the slider's name as a variable is redrawn as it moves (a vector field is drawn once, at the slider's starting value). Use a slider when what the section is about is how something changes as a parameter varies: the reader dragging it and watching the picture respond is something prose can only describe. A complete example, for the syntax only:
[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: what this graph shows
xlabel: x
ylabel: y
xrange: -4, 4
trace: s*x | label: family member
point: 2, 2*s | label: P
segment: 0, 0, 2, 2*s | dashed: true
slider: s | range: -3, 3 | init: 1 | step: 0.1
[/GRAPH]
  function2d also supports filled regions, repeatable within a block:
fill: upper_expression, lower_expression | range: start, end | label: caption | color: optional | opacity: 0.22
  Both boundaries use x and calculator notation; write 0 for the horizontal axis, or constants for rectangle heights. The required range gives the horizontal endpoints. Boundaries and endpoints may use sliders and update as they move. label, color and opacity are optional; opacity is between 0 and 1. Fill is behind curves and marks. Draw the boundary traces separately when their outlines matter. Use fills for areas under or between curves, signed contributions, Riemann rectangles, and accumulation strips. Split at crossings or sign changes and use separate colors and labels when the distinction matters; shading itself is geometric and does not encode the sign of an integral. Sampling does not prove continuity or detect every discontinuity, so choose intervals where the boundaries are finite and continuous. Do not use fill with parametric2d, vectorfield2d or surface3d.

  Expressions are self-contained: there are no user-defined functions, so a quantity built from another curve is written out in full, in terms of x (or t) and the slider names.

  A graph is part of the exposition, so it follows the same rules as the prose around it. It may show the instances the text works through and the general shape of the objects involved; it must not plot the specific object a nearby question asks about, mark that question's answer, or otherwise do the reader's work for it. It should earn its place: take the graph away and the surrounding prose should lose something. Mark the points the prose actually computes with, draw the segments the prose names, and use a slider when the prose compares many members of one family. One graph per idea is plenty; don't plot the same object twice, and keep a plot to a handful of curves so it stays readable. The block sits on its own lines between paragraphs, like a table.

  Every field on its own "key: value" line. title/xlabel/ylabel/zlabel are always optional but should usually be filled in. The range requirements depend on the type: function2d needs xrange (yrange is optional — left out, the vertical window is fitted to the curves, so give it only when a specific window matters), parametric2d needs trange (xrange and yrange are optional there too), and surface3d and vectorfield2d need both xrange and yrange. Pick bounds that actually show what the graph is for, the way a chosen numeric example elsewhere in this document is chosen to land on its point, not a generic default. function2d and parametric2d can repeat the trace line for more than one curve on the same axes; surface3d and vectorfield2d take exactly one z (or one u and one v) — nothing to repeat there. label and color on a trace line are both optional. A parametric2d trace line packs both components into one line, comma-separated: trace: cos(t), sin(t) | label: .... The fields of a line are separated by " | " with a space on each side, exactly as in a table row.

  Every expression (trace, z, u, v, and the coordinates of a point or segment) is evaluated as a plain math expression by a separate library, not typeset by KaTeX — write x^2, sin(x), sqrt(x^2 + y^2), atan2(y, x), abs(x) in ordinary calculator-style notation (abs(x), not |x| — bars aren't valid syntax here), never inside \( \) and never with LaTeX commands like \sin or \frac{}{}. Captions are the opposite, with one wrinkle. The title and the label on a trace go through the normal KaTeX pass like anything else in this document, so \( \) works there exactly as it would in a sentence. The xlabel, the ylabel, and the label on a point or a segment are drawn inside the plot itself, where a label must be either one single \( ... \) span (the whole label is math) or plain text with no math in it; never mix prose and a math span in one of those, and keep them short. The zlabel is plain text. Keep the two apart — an expression written in LaTeX syntax won't evaluate, and a label written in plain-expression syntax just won't typeset.

LANGUAGE
Write every lesson in English. Use === SECTION N: TITLE === section headings. Keep QUESTION, ANSWER, BONUS, TABLE, TIMELINE, GRAPH and graph field names in their literal parser syntax.


CONTEXT
The larger subject is tree.topic.
The learning goal and boundaries are the current node’s explanation.
Use the labels and explanations of all the current node’s requires as already-taught background. With no requires, this is an entry topic; respect any calibrated starting knowledge stated in explanation.
Do not introduce material belonging to later nodes that require this one.


DOCUMENT STRUCTURE

Organize sections around coherent learning steps in the subject. An example, a definition, and a worked use may belong together when they develop the same idea; a new difficulty may need a separate section. There is no section quota. Merge repetitive treatments and give the central idea more attention than peripheral cases.

Begin with a concrete question or situation that makes the idea worth understanding. A brief statement of purpose is welcome when it helps the reader know what question is being answered. Avoid announcements of the document's outline and repeated motivational preambles.

Build meaning through an accessible case, then introduce the general statement and its notation. Explain each new symbol's role and how to read the whole expression; do not assume a displayed formula explains itself. Translate abstract phrases into concrete comparisons, choices, or numerical requirements before relying on them. Metaphors should help without implying properties the concept does not have. Use a contrasting case when it resolves a likely misconception.

Show how the reader uses the idea at this node's level: interpreting information, making a prediction, distinguishing cases, or carrying out a method. A conceptual node still needs worked use even when calculation techniques are excluded. Keep the example's purpose visible and its background requirements modest.

Match justification to the learning goal. Derive a method when understanding its derivation is part of the scope; explain the reason behind a conceptual claim at a level the reader can follow. Definitions need meaning and examples rather than a manufactured proof. State the relevant assumptions and avoid unsupported leaps, but do not prove every non-trivial assertion merely because it is possible to do so. In an informal lesson, a short explanation of why a pattern persists may suffice. Clearly distinguish what sampled data suggest from what a stated rule guarantees, without letting that distinction dominate the first encounter with the idea.

Introduce supporting contrasts after the central idea is secure. Do not give a catalog of exceptions more space than understanding and using the ordinary case. Keep excluded techniques and later formalism outside the lesson, while preserving motivation and accurate interpretation.

A visual must agree with the mathematical or factual object described. Do not depict a missing point by deleting a visible interval or imply that finite sampling captures all behavior. Use only supported graph features. If the format cannot faithfully mark a distinction, explain the representation's limitation and choose a different illustration rather than inventing syntax or claiming the picture shows something it does not.

Scatter your main questions throughout the document, embedded at the natural moment right after the concept or technique they test has just been introduced. A question about a definition should appear right after that definition, while it is fresh. A question about a derived result should appear immediately after the derivation. Questions should feel like a natural pause in the reading — "try this now" — not a separate block at the end. Do not group them, do not create a separate exercises section, do not label them "Practice Set" anything. Once a question is posed, nothing else in the document — not the sentences leading into it, not the transition that follows it, no matter how far downstream — may discuss, justify, hint at, or evaluate its answer or any of its options. One disguise of this is easy to miss while writing it: a reflective aside, introduced as "worth noting" or "worth pausing on," that revisits why a particular wrong option might have looked tempting. Framing it as a general observation doesn't change what it is — it's still explaining one of the question's own options, and it counts the same as putting that explanation directly beneath the question. The reader can scroll ahead or back freely, so anything said nearby about why a choice is right or wrong is visible before, or instead of, working it out. After a question, move forward into the next new piece of content; don't loop back to recap, defend, or unpack what was just tested. Just use the [QUESTION N] format inline, numbered consecutively in the order they appear. Everything about what makes a good question, once you're at the point of writing one, is collected under QUESTION CONSTRUCTION RULES below — read it before drafting your first one.

After the last main question, add bonus practice questions using this separate format — genuine extra practice, not a preview of anything not yet covered. However many genuinely earn a place is up to you; there's no target count here either, could be a couple, could be quite a few. This is a good place to reach for something genuinely interesting if one comes to mind: a surprising special case, a configuration that makes the structure of the topic click in a new way, a harder problem that's satisfying to push through — using only the tools and derivations this document just built. Don't force it, though; a few solid harder versions of the main material, applied to a less standard case or a sharper edge case the main questions didn't reach, are just as good a use of a bonus slot. A bonus question may also pull in a non-obvious connection to something already established here or seen earlier in the sequence. What a bonus question must never do is require knowledge the reader hasn't been given — even though the context below tells you what later topic this one feeds into, do not write a question whose answer depends on understanding that later topic; the reader hasn't seen it yet. This includes facts that feel like a small, natural step from what's already established: if the document never actually states or demonstrates it, even once, it hasn't been given, no matter how obvious the step feels while writing it — a reader who hasn't had that exact leap modeled for them has no way to know it's expected. Gesturing at a real-world structure or application this machinery is used for elsewhere is fine as flavor in the setup, but the question itself must be fully answerable using only what this document derived.

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: X]
Question text here.

(A) option
(B) option
(C) option
(D) option
(E) option
[/BONUS]

Replace X with the correct letter, same as for main questions above. The answer tag is hidden from the reader and used only for feedback. Same question construction rules apply as for the main questions.


QUESTION CONSTRUCTION RULES (guidelines, not a bureaucratic checklist — use judgment, and read this in full before drafting your first question)

A question is only doing its job if answering it takes something the reader doesn't already have in hand: a new instance to work through, a real decision to make, or a step of reasoning nobody has spelled out for them yet. Simplicity is never the problem — a well-crafted simple question beats a convoluted one every time, and for a simple topic a straightforward question is usually the right call. Restating is the problem: if a question can be answered from memory of the sentence sitting directly above it, it isn't testing anything. What follows are the specific, recognizable shapes that failure takes in practice. Check every drafted question against all of them before moving on.

FRESH WORK AT THE RIGHT LEVEL. A question must leave meaningful work for the reader rather than repeat a specific answer already supplied. Early checks may use a familiar structure with new values when the task is to learn how to read notation or carry out a first application. Later checks should require a fresh interpretation, a choice between cases, a correction of a mistaken claim, or transfer to a different setup. Do not demand a new kind of object for every question: that can introduce difficulty unrelated to the goal. Across the lesson, include both accessible checks and genuine transfer. Keep all questions answerable with established knowledge.
HANDED-OVER REASONING. If solving a question requires some intermediate fact that follows from the given setup by a short, easy step, make the reader work that out — don't state it in the question. This is different from genuinely given data (measurements, constants, configuration the reader has no other way to know), which should stay. The same goes for the reasoning path itself, not just quantities: if the stem already spells out the specific relationship, mechanism, or formula that leads to the answer, it has done the reader's thinking for them, and all that's left is a plug-in. This has a common, easy-to-spot shape: the prose derives some formula or relationship, and the very next question opens by restating that same formula before asking the reader to apply it — "Using [the thing just derived], find/compute/determine..." Don't open or frame a question that way, and don't re-serve an already-established result in the stem at all; trust the reader to recall it unprompted. If several established results are legitimately in play and naming them is genuinely needed for clarity, pair that naming with a real decision the reader still has to make (which case applies, what sign or direction is correct, how two pieces combine), so recalling the tool is only the entry ticket, not the whole task.

TEST THE INTENDED ABILITY. Judge a question by the learning goal, not by the number of calculations or decision points. A simple substitution or identification may be appropriate for an initial check if it tests a newly learned interpretation. It is insufficient as the only evidence of conceptual understanding. Include questions where the options distinguish explanations, representations, assumptions, or cases, so success requires more than recognizing the wording of the preceding paragraph.
BYPASSABLE CONCEPT. For complex or subtle topics, aim for questions where understanding the material is genuinely required: a conceptual trap, a case where the obvious mechanical approach fails, a need to identify which principle applies before proceeding at all. For simpler topics, straightforward questions are fine and often better — don't manufacture complexity where none exists. Either way, check this concretely before finalizing a question built around a specific technique or identity: is there a different, more direct path to the same answer that skips the technique entirely — computing the raw result by hand instead of applying what the section just built, say — and is that bypass at least as easy? If so, the question isn't testing the thing it's attached to, however relevant it looks on the page. Reshape the setup so the technique is genuinely the fastest or only reasonable route, or don't ask it.

CONCISENESS. State what's given and what's being asked, then stop. Re-explaining context the reader already has, narrating the setup instead of presenting it, and announcing which tool to reach for before the reader's had a chance to reach for it themselves are all padding, not clarity — cut them. This applies to answer options too: once the stem has already fixed an ordering, a variable name, or a piece of notation, repeating it in front of every single option adds nothing — give the value alone and let the stem carry what it represents.

DISTRACTORS. Should be clearly wrong on reflection; for mathematical questions, avoid options that are equivalent in value even if written differently, and never duplicate an option outright. When a question's real content is that some quantity turns out to be independent of a variable that looks like it should matter — the same for every case, every index, every choice of an otherwise-free parameter — that independence claim is exactly what a distractor should test: include at least one option representing what the value would be if it did depend on that variable, not just numeric variants clustered around the right magnitude. Otherwise the question can be answered by guessing "it's probably the boring constant one" without ever engaging with why it's constant.

GETTING THE TARGET RIGHT. Some questions hinge on a distinction that's easy to get backwards by accident — which of two similar things is which, which direction a relationship or cause runs, what happened before what, which side an effect lands on, what gets added versus subtracted. When a question's correct answer depends on a choice like this, work it out deliberately and double-check it before finalizing — this is the single most common way a question quietly drifts toward the wrong answer without anyone noticing while drafting. And if a question's content is naturally tied to material that only exists in one particular section, confirm before committing to that placement that some natural, non-contrived choice of values or configuration there can actually produce a clean, defensible answer; if it can't, look for freedom you haven't used yet — a relative sign or magnitude, a direction, which object plays which role, which specific case you reach for — before forcing a strained setup.

FINAL REVIEW — before treating the document as finished, reread it once, straight through, in the order a reader will actually meet it. Everything above is written to be applied while drafting each piece — a section, a question, a table — and checking a piece against a rule while writing it will not catch a problem that only exists in how two pieces relate to each other across a distance. That's what this pass is for: read it the way a first-time reader would, start to end, and watch for failures that are invisible piece-by-piece but obvious once the whole thing is visible at once.

- Forward references: does any question, or any tool block, depend on a formula, definition, or result that doesn't actually appear until later in the document? A question may only use what a reader would have already seen by that exact point in the reading order — not what's coming a section, or even a paragraph, later. This is easy to miss while drafting a question right after writing the paragraph that motivates it, since the formula it needs feels close by even when it hasn't been derived yet.
- Does the opening give the central idea a meaningful purpose? Are brief explanations of purpose useful rather than repeated announcements? Can a first-time reader follow the progression without already knowing the conclusion?
- Does the central statement have a clear meaning, explained notation, an accessible example, and worked use? Is its justification appropriate to the scope, without unsupported claims or premature formalism?
- Do questions leave real work at the intended level, progressing from accessible checks to fresh interpretation or transfer? Are any questions merely repeating an answer already given, or introducing unfamiliar machinery to manufacture difficulty?
- No "using the ___" openers anywhere, and no stem that restates an already-derived tool right before asking the reader to apply it.
- No paragraph anywhere in the document — before a question, immediately after it, or much later, however it's framed — that discusses, defends, hints at, or explains why a specific option is right or wrong.
- Every bonus question's reasoning traceable to something the main document actually stated or demonstrated on the page — not a natural-feeling extension of it that was never actually shown.
- Every main and bonus question has exactly one [ANSWER: X] tag naming a letter that is actually one of that question's own listed options — a missing, mistyped, or dangling tag means that question silently fails to score.
- Every section whose central object has a shape: does it have a graph, placed where the section first works with that object? A section about a visible object that is explained in prose alone is a gap to fix now.
- Do wording and visuals avoid misleading implications? Do plots faithfully represent the described domain and features, with limitations acknowledged when the supported format cannot show a distinction?
- Every graph block: expressions in plain calculator notation (no LaTeX, no bars for absolute value, ^ for powers); every slider name used in an expression is defined by a slider line; ranges that actually show the feature the prose is about; no graph plots or marks the specific object a nearby question asks about; xlabel, ylabel, point and segment labels are each one math span or plain text, never a mix; fields separated by " | " with spaces.
- No literal "|" sitting inside a table cell outside \lvert \rvert.

If the read-through turns up any of these, fix it before finalizing. Having applied a rule correctly while drafting a piece is not the same guarantee as the finished document actually being right — the read-through is what confirms it, not an assumption that following the rules along the way was enough.

nodes.label: Bras, Kets, and Outer Products
nodes.explanation: Translate complex vectors and linear maps into bra-ket notation, distinguishing the scalar inner product from the operator outer product. Build and apply a rank-one projector in a two-dimensional example. Assume the calibrated ability to use complex-conjugate inner products, normalized vectors, and matrix eigenvectors; introduce the notation explicitly rather than reteaching those calculations. Leave changes of basis and the measurement postulate to their own lessons.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: A vector and its matching bra ===

Suppose a calculation repeatedly asks for the component of one complex vector along another. Writing every column and conjugate row soon hides which object is a vector and which operation produces a number. Bra-ket notation makes those roles visible without changing the underlying linear algebra.

A ket, written \( |u\rangle \), is a vector. In a specified two-dimensional coordinate system it can be represented by a column. Its matching bra, written \( \langle u| \), is the conjugate-transpose row. For example,

\[
|u\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\langle u|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The letter identifies the vector; the surrounding marks identify its role in the calculation. Forming the bra conjugates the coefficients as well as changing the column into a row. In particular, if \( |w\rangle=c|u\rangle \), then \( \langle w|=c^*\langle u| \), where the star means complex conjugation.

Putting a bra to the left of a ket gives the inner product \( \langle u|v\rangle \), a scalar. With \( |v\rangle=(\sqrt{3}/2,1/2)^{\mathsf T} \), row-by-column multiplication gives

\[
\langle u|v\rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}-i}{2\sqrt{2}}.
\]

Reversing the order of the vectors conjugates the result: \( \langle v|u\rangle=\langle u|v\rangle^* \). The expression \( \langle u|u\rangle \) is the squared norm, so a normalized vector satisfies \( \langle u|u\rangle=1 \). This notation preserves the familiar rule that the inner product is conjugate-linear in its first vector and linear in its second.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: B]
The ket \( |w\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2i,1-i)^{\mathsf T} \) is given. Which row is \( \langle w| \)?

(A) \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2i,1-i) \)
(B) \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(-2i,1+i) \)
(C) \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(-2i,1-i) \)
(D) \( \frac{1}{6}(-2i,1+i) \)
(E) \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2i,1+i) \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: Reversing the order builds a map ===

The outer product \( |u\rangle\langle v| \) has a different type from the inner product. A column multiplied by a row is a matrix. It takes an input vector, extracts a scalar with the bra, and multiplies the ket by that scalar:

\[
\bigl(|u\rangle\langle v|\bigr)|z\rangle
=|u\rangle\langle v|z\rangle.
\]

The scalar \( \langle v|z\rangle \) tells us how much of \( |u\rangle \) the map returns. For instance, choose \( |a\rangle=(1,0)^{\mathsf T} \) and \( |b\rangle=(1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{2} \). Their outer product and its action on an arbitrary input are

\[
|a\rangle\langle b|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\bigl(|a\rangle\langle b|\bigr)
\begin{pmatrix}z_1\\z_2\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{z_1-iz_2}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Every output is along the first coordinate direction, although the scalar depends on both input coordinates. When both defining vectors are nonzero, the outer product has rank one: its possible outputs span just one direction.

An operator \( A \) can also appear between a bra and a ket. The expression \( \langle v|A|z\rangle \) means first apply \( A \) to the ket and then take the inner product with \( |v\rangle \). It is a scalar. Tracking the type of each object helps prevent meaningless multiplications.

[TABLE]
Expression | Object produced | Coordinate operation
\( \langle v|z\rangle \) | Scalar | Row times column
\( |u\rangle\langle v| \) | Operator | Column times row
\( A|z\rangle \) | Ket | Matrix times column
\( \langle v|A|z\rangle \) | Scalar | Row times matrix times column
[/TABLE]

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: D]
Let \( |r\rangle=(1,0)^{\mathsf T} \) and \( |s\rangle=(0,i)^{\mathsf T} \). Which pair gives \( \langle r|s\rangle \) and \( |r\rangle\langle s| \), in that order?

(A) \( 0,\begin{pmatrix}0&i\\0&0\end{pmatrix} \)
(B) \( i,\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\0&0\end{pmatrix} \)
(C) \( 0,\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\i&0\end{pmatrix} \)
(D) \( 0,\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\0&0\end{pmatrix} \)
(E) \( 1,\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: Building a rank-one projector ===

A projection keeps the part of a vector along a chosen direction. For normalized \( |u\rangle \), define

\[
P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|.
\]

Its action is \( P_u|z\rangle=\langle u|z\rangle|u\rangle \). It returns \( |u\rangle \) unchanged and sends any vector orthogonal to \( |u\rangle \) to zero. Applying it twice changes nothing after the first application:

\[
P_u^2=|u\rangle\underbrace{\langle u|u\rangle}_{1}\langle u|=P_u.
\]

This property is called idempotence. Here the projection is orthogonal in the complex-inner-product sense. No rule about physical measurement is needed to construct or apply this linear map.

For the normalized vector \( |u\rangle=(1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{2} \) from the opening example,

\[
P_u=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\i&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
P_u\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The output need not be normalized. Its purpose is to retain a component, including its magnitude, rather than rescale every input into a unit vector.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: A]
Let \( |a\rangle=(1,-i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{2} \) and \( |z\rangle=(1,2i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{5} \). What is \( |a\rangle\langle a|z\rangle \)?

(A) \( \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}(-1,i)^{\mathsf T} \)
(B) \( \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}(3,-3i)^{\mathsf T} \)
(C) \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-1,i)^{\mathsf T} \)
(D) \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(1,2i)^{\mathsf T} \)
(E) \( -\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \)
[/QUESTION]

If a direction is supplied by a nonzero vector \( |w\rangle \) that is not normalized, the projection is instead

\[
P=\frac{|w\rangle\langle w|}{\langle w|w\rangle}.
\]

The denominator removes the vector's arbitrary squared scale. This follows either by first normalizing the vector or by checking that the resulting map acts as the identity on \( |w\rangle \).

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: C]
A calculation labels \( Q=|w\rangle\langle w| \) a projector, with \( |w\rangle=(1,1)^{\mathsf T} \). Which correction makes it the orthogonal projector onto that direction?

(A) No correction; \( Q^2=Q \).
(B) Replace it by \( \sqrt{2}Q \).
(C) Replace it by \( Q/2 \).
(D) Replace it by \( Q/\sqrt{2} \).
(E) Replace it by \( 2Q \).
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: E]
Let \( |v\rangle=(2,i)^{\mathsf T} \) and \( |z\rangle=(i,1)^{\mathsf T} \). What does the orthogonal projector onto the direction of \( |v\rangle \) return when applied to \( |z\rangle \)?

(A) \( (2i,-1)^{\mathsf T} \)
(B) \( (6i,-3)^{\mathsf T}/5 \)
(C) \( (2i,1)^{\mathsf T}/5 \)
(D) \( (i,1)^{\mathsf T} \)
(E) \( (2i,-1)^{\mathsf T}/5 \)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Adjoints and Hermitian Operators
nodes.explanation: Calculate an adjoint and determine whether a finite matrix is Hermitian, then explain why Hermitian eigenvalues are real and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal. Use small complex matrices and distinguish Hermitian from merely real or symmetric. Assume the calibrated complex inner products and matrix eigenvalue skills. Establish the finite-dimensional result here; differential-operator boundary conditions and physical measurement rules come later.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: Moving a matrix across an inner product ===

Suppose you know two complex vectors and want to compare one with the result of applying a matrix to the other. Can you move the matrix to the first vector without changing the comparison? This question leads to the adjoint, and then to a class of matrices whose eigenvalues are guaranteed to be real.

Use the complex inner product convention \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\): conjugate the entries of the first column vector, turn it into a row, and multiply by the second vector. The first position is conjugate-linear, while the second is linear. Even multiplication by \(i\) shows why this matters: \(\langle u,iv\rangle=i\langle u,v\rangle\), whereas \(\langle iu,v\rangle=-i\langle u,v\rangle\). Moving an operation to the first position requires care with conjugation.

For a matrix \(A\), its adjoint \(A^\dagger\) is its conjugate transpose:
\[
A^\dagger=\overline{A}^{\mathsf T},\qquad (A^\dagger)_{jk}=\overline{A_{kj}}.
\]
The bar conjugates each complex entry, and the transpose exchanges rows and columns. Thus the entry formerly in row \(k\), column \(j\) moves to row \(j\), column \(k\) and is conjugated. You may transpose first or conjugate first; the result is the same.

For example,
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1+i&2\\ i&-1\end{pmatrix}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}1-i&-i\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The upper-right entry of the adjoint comes from the lower-left entry of the original matrix. Conjugation changes that \(i\) to \(-i\). The real entries keep their values but still change positions when required by the transpose. Applying the adjoint operation twice returns the original matrix.

The reason this operation matters is the identity
\[
\langle u,Av\rangle=\langle A^\dagger u,v\rangle.
\]
It says that applying \(A\) to the second vector has the same effect on the inner product as applying \(A^\dagger\) to the first. In matrix notation, the right side is \((A^\dagger u)^\dagger v=u^\dagger Av\), exactly the left side. Merely transposing generally misses the conjugation needed for this identity.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: C]
What is the adjoint of \(B=\begin{pmatrix}2i&1+i\\-3&4-i\end{pmatrix}\)?

(A) \(\begin{pmatrix}2i&-3\\1+i&4-i\end{pmatrix}\)
(B) \(\begin{pmatrix}-2i&1-i\\-3&4+i\end{pmatrix}\)
(C) \(\begin{pmatrix}-2i&-3\\1-i&4+i\end{pmatrix}\)
(D) \(\begin{pmatrix}-2i&1+i\\-3&4+i\end{pmatrix}\)
(E) \(\begin{pmatrix}2i&-3\\1-i&4+i\end{pmatrix}\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: Recognizing a Hermitian matrix ===

A square matrix \(H\) is Hermitian when it equals its own adjoint:
\[
H^\dagger=H.
\]
For such a matrix, the inner-product identity becomes \(\langle u,Hv\rangle=\langle Hu,v\rangle\). The same operation can move between the two positions.

The entry condition is \(H_{jk}=\overline{H_{kj}}\). On the diagonal, this requires an entry to equal its own conjugate, so every diagonal entry is real. Away from the diagonal, entries reflected across the diagonal must be complex conjugates. They need not be real or equal to each other.

For example,
\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}2&i\\-i&2\end{pmatrix}
\]
is Hermitian: its diagonal entries are real, and its two off-diagonal entries are conjugates. Yet it is neither a real matrix nor a symmetric matrix, since its transpose differs from itself.

These three tests ask different questions.

[TABLE]
Property | Test | What is checked
Real | \(\overline{A}=A\) | Each entry is real
Symmetric | \(A^{\mathsf T}=A\) | Reflected entries are equal
Hermitian | \(A^\dagger=A\) | Reflected entries are conjugates
[/TABLE]

For a real matrix, conjugation changes nothing, so Hermitian and symmetric are equivalent. Real entries alone do not ensure symmetry. For example, \(\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is real but is not Hermitian. Complex symmetry alone is also insufficient: \(\begin{pmatrix}1&i\\i&4\end{pmatrix}\) equals its transpose, but its off-diagonal entries do not meet the conjugate-pair requirement.

In a small matrix, checking the diagonal entries and one entry from each reflected pair is enough. There is no need to calculate eigenvalues to decide whether the matrix is Hermitian.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: A]
The parameters \(a,b,c\) are real. Which condition is necessary and sufficient for \(M=\begin{pmatrix}a+bi&2+ci\\2-3i&5\end{pmatrix}\) to be Hermitian?

(A) \(b=0\) and \(c=3\), with \(a\) unrestricted.
(B) \(b=0\) and \(c=-3\), with \(a\) unrestricted.
(C) \(b=1\) and \(c=3\), with \(a\) unrestricted.
(D) \(a=5\), \(b=0\), and \(c=3\).
(E) \(b=0\) and \(c=0\), with \(a\) unrestricted.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: Why the eigenvalues are real ===

Return to \(H=\begin{pmatrix}2&i\\-i&2\end{pmatrix}\). Its entries include imaginary numbers, but its characteristic equation is
\[
\det(H-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)^2-i(-i)=(2-\lambda)^2-1=0.
\]
Its eigenvalues are therefore \(1\) and \(3\). This computation illustrates the result; the Hermitian condition provides a guarantee that applies to every finite Hermitian matrix.

To see why, take any eigenvector \(v\ne0\) with \(Hv=\lambda v\). At this stage, allow \(\lambda\) to be complex. Linearity in the second position gives
\[
\langle v,Hv\rangle=\lambda\langle v,v\rangle.
\]
Because \(H\) is Hermitian, moving it to the first position leaves the inner product unchanged. Conjugate-linearity in that position gives
\[
\langle v,Hv\rangle=\langle Hv,v\rangle
=\overline{\lambda}\langle v,v\rangle.
\]
Combining the two expressions yields
\[
(\lambda-\overline{\lambda})\langle v,v\rangle=0.
\]
The squared norm \(\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2\) is strictly positive because an eigenvector is nonzero. We can divide by it, leaving \(\lambda=\overline{\lambda}\). A complex number equals its conjugate exactly when its imaginary part vanishes. Thus every eigenvalue of a finite Hermitian matrix is real.

The argument does not require a normalized eigenvector. Rescaling an eigenvector by any nonzero complex scalar \(d\) leaves its eigenvalue unchanged: \(H(dv)=dHv=\lambda(dv)\). Normalization changes a vector's length, not the eigenvalue attached to its direction. Also, the zero vector cannot replace \(v\) in the argument: its squared norm vanishes, and it is not an eigenvector.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: D]
A Hermitian matrix \(H\) and a nonzero vector \(v\) satisfy \(Hv=(6+bi)v\), where \(b\) is real. Let \(w=(2-i)v\). Which statement must hold?

(A) \(b=0\) and \(Hw=6(2-i)w\).
(B) \(b\) is unrestricted and \(Hw=(6+bi)w\).
(C) \(b=0\) and \(Hw=-6w\).
(D) \(b=0\) and \(Hw=6w\).
(E) \(b=0\) and \(Hw=6\sqrt{5}\,w\).
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: Distinct eigenvalues force orthogonality ===

Consider the real symmetric, hence Hermitian, matrix \(R=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\). It stretches the direction of \(u=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}\) by a factor of \(4\), since \(Ru=4u\). It stretches the direction of \(v=(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}\) by a factor of \(2\), since \(Rv=2v\). The two eigendirections are perpendicular.

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: Perpendicular eigendirections of a real Hermitian matrix
xlabel: \(x\)
ylabel: \(y\)
xrange: -1.4, 1.4
yrange: -1.4, 1.4
aspect: equal
trace: x | label: Direction of \(u\)
trace: -x | label: Direction of \(v\)
point: 1, 1 | label: \(u\)
point: 1, -1 | label: \(v\)
segment: 0, 0, 1, 1
segment: 0, 0, 1, -1
[/GRAPH]

Their inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle=1-1=0\). For complex vectors, orthogonality still means a zero inner product, with conjugation included. A general complex vector cannot be represented faithfully by one arrow in this real coordinate plane; the inner product is the test that applies in either case.

Now let \(Hu=\lambda u\) and \(Hv=\mu v\) for eigenvectors of any finite Hermitian matrix. The eigenvalues \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) are real, as established above. Evaluate the same inner product in two ways:
\[
\langle u,Hv\rangle=\mu\langle u,v\rangle,
\qquad
\langle Hu,v\rangle=\lambda\langle u,v\rangle.
\]
Hermiticity makes the left sides equal, so
\[
(\mu-\lambda)\langle u,v\rangle=0.
\]
If the eigenvalues are distinct, \(\mu-\lambda\ne0\), forcing \(\langle u,v\rangle=0\). This is why eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix are orthogonal. The claim applies to any nonzero multiples of those eigenvectors, not just vectors of unit length.

The word distinct is essential. With equal eigenvalues, the equation becomes \(0=0\) and imposes no restriction on the overlap. For instance, every nonzero vector is an eigenvector of \(2I\) with eigenvalue \(2\). The vectors \((1,0)^{\mathsf T}\) and \((1,1)^{\mathsf T}\) are both examples, yet their inner product is \(1\). Hermiticity does not require every possible pair of eigenvectors to be orthogonal.

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: B]
A two-dimensional Hermitian matrix has eigenvector \(u=(1,i)^{\mathsf T}\) with eigenvalue \(-2\), and eigenvector \(v=(z,2)^{\mathsf T}\) with eigenvalue \(5\). What is \(z\)?

(A) \(-2i\)
(B) \(2i\)
(C) \(2\)
(D) \(-2\)
(E) \(0\)
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: E]
What are the eigenvalues of \(K=\begin{pmatrix}1&1+2i\\1-2i&1\end{pmatrix}\)?

(A) \(1-5\) and \(1+5\)
(B) \(-\sqrt{6}\) and \(\sqrt{6}\)
(C) \(1-\sqrt{3}\) and \(1+\sqrt{3}\)
(D) \(1-i\sqrt{5}\) and \(1+i\sqrt{5}\)
(E) \(1-\sqrt{5}\) and \(1+\sqrt{5}\)
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 2]
[ANSWER: C]
Let \(H=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,-1)\), \(u=(1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}\), and \(v=(1,1,0)^{\mathsf T}\). Which pair gives their common eigenvalue and their inner product \(\langle u,v\rangle\), in that order?

(A) \(2,\ 1+i\)
(B) \(-1,\ 1-i\)
(C) \(2,\ 1-i\)
(D) \(2,\ 0\)
(E) \(-1,\ 0\)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Commutators and Operator Identities
nodes.explanation: Manipulate noncommuting products without changing their order, using commutator linearity and the product identities. Start with two explicit matrices, then practise deriving [N,a†]=a† from [a,a†]=I and N=a†a, without assuming oscillator physics. Assume ordinary matrix multiplication and algebra. The goal is reliable operator calculation; angular-momentum spectra and oscillator energy quantization are separate applications.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: WHEN ORDER CHANGES THE RESULT ===

Two operations can use the same ingredients and still give different results when their order changes. For matrices, the question is concrete: what remains when we subtract the product in one order from the product in the other?

Consider the two square matrices
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Ordinary matrix multiplication gives
\[
AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Their difference is
\[
AB-BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\-2&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This difference measures the failure of the two products to agree. It is called the commutator of \(A\) and \(B\), written
\[
[A,B]=AB-BA.
\]
The brackets name a new matrix or operator; they are not ordinary parentheses. The first term keeps the bracket order, and the second reverses it. An operator acts on a vector, and a product such as \(AB\) means that \(B\) acts first and \(A\) acts second.

The equation \([A,B]=0\) means \(AB=BA\): the operators commute. Here \(0\) denotes the zero matrix or zero operator. All matrix products in this lesson use square matrices of the same size. For general operators, assume the displayed products are defined on a common set of vectors where the stated identities hold.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: C]
Let \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\). What is \([P,Q]\)?

(A) \(\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
(B) \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-6\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
(C) \(\begin{pmatrix}0&6\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
(D) \(\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
(E) \(\begin{pmatrix}0&6\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: ADDING AND SCALING COMMUTATORS ===

The definition provides several shortcuts without allowing us to swap factors inside a product. Reversing the bracket order changes the sign:
\[
[B,A]=BA-AB=-[A,B].
\]
An operator commutes with itself because \([A,A]=AA-AA=0\). The identity operator \(I\), which leaves every vector unchanged, also commutes with every operator: \([A,I]=AI-IA=A-A=0\).

Commutators distribute over sums and allow scalar coefficients to come outside. If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are ordinary numbers, then
\[
[\alpha A+\beta B,C]=\alpha[A,C]+\beta[B,C],
\]
\[
[A,\alpha B+\beta C]=\alpha[A,B]+\beta[A,C].
\]
For example, expanding the definition gives
\[
[A,B+C]=A(B+C)-(B+C)A=AB+AC-BA-CA.
\]
Grouping the two differences produces \([A,B]+[A,C]\). We have rearranged terms in a sum, which is allowed; we have not rearranged factors within a product.

Suppose \([R,S]=T\). A worked reduction is
\[
[R,4S-2R+5I]=4[R,S]-2[R,R]+5[R,I]=4T.
\]
The coefficients are scalars. An operator coefficient cannot generally be pulled outside the bracket in the same way.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: A]
Suppose \([P,Q]=C\ne0\). What is \([3P+2Q,2P-Q]\)?

(A) \(-7C\)
(B) \(C\)
(C) \(-C\)
(D) \(-5C\)
(E) \(7C\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: COMMUTATORS THROUGH PRODUCTS ===

A product inside a bracket needs a different rule from a sum. To calculate \([A,BC]\), insert two opposite terms in the definition:
\[
[A,BC]=ABC-BCA=ABC-BAC+BAC-BCA.
\]
Factoring each adjacent pair gives
\[
[A,BC]=[A,B]C+B[A,C].
\]
The factor \(C\) remains to the right of the first commutator, and \(B\) remains to the left of the second. Their positions come from the expansion, rather than from a choice of convenient ordering.

There is also a product rule for the first slot:
\[
[AB,C]=ABC-CAB=ABC-ACB+ACB-CAB,
\]
so
\[
[AB,C]=A[B,C]+[A,C]B.
\]
In each rule, there are two terms because the commutator can act on either factor of the product. These identities apply without assuming that any of the operators commute.

For a worked example, suppose \([R,S]=2I\) and \([R,T]=S\). Then
\[
[R,ST]=[R,S]T+S[R,T]=(2I)T+SS=2T+S^2.
\]
The notation \(S^2\) means \(SS\), just as for a matrix power.

A repeated factor does not automatically make the two product-rule terms equal. In particular,
\[
[A,B^2]=[A,B]B+B[A,B].
\]
This can be written as \(2B[A,B]\) only if \(B\) commutes with \([A,B]\). If that extra relation has not been established, retain both ordered terms. To handle a longer product, apply the appropriate product rule again to the remaining product.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: B]
Suppose \([P,R]=0\) and \([Q,R]=K\), with no further commutation relations given. Which expression is guaranteed to equal \([PQ,R^2]\)?

(A) \(PKR\)
(B) \(P(KR+RK)\)
(C) \((KR+RK)P\)
(D) \(2PKR\)
(E) \(-P(KR+RK)\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: AN ABSTRACT OPERATOR CALCULATION ===

We can now work from an operator relation without knowing entries of any matrices. Let two abstract operators satisfy
\[
[a,a^\dagger]=I,
\]
and define
\[
N=a^\dagger a.
\]
The symbol \(a^\dagger\) is read as "a dagger." It usually denotes the adjoint of \(a\); here we need only the supplied commutator relation and the definition of \(N\). These are abstract operators, and we do not assume that they have finite matrix representations.

As a worked calculation, find the commutator of \(N\) with \(a\). First, reversing the supplied bracket gives \([a^\dagger,a]=-I\). Applying the product rule to the definition of \(N\) gives
\[
[N,a]=[a^\dagger a,a]=a^\dagger[a,a]+[a^\dagger,a]a.
\]
The first commutator vanishes, while the second is the reversed supplied relation. Therefore
\[
[N,a]=a^\dagger 0+(-I)a=-a.
\]
Every reduction has preserved the order of the remaining factors. The supplied relation replaces a difference of products; it does not permit us to exchange \(a\) and \(a^\dagger\) without a correction.

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: B]
What is \([N,a^\dagger]\) for these operators?

(A) \(0\)
(B) \(a^\dagger\)
(C) \(a\)
(D) \(-a^\dagger\)
(E) \(I\)
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: D]
Suppose \([R,S]=T\) and \([R,T]=0\). Which expression is guaranteed to equal \([R^2,S]\)?

(A) \(T^2\)
(B) \(RT\)
(C) \(2R^2T\)
(D) \(2RT\)
(E) \(-2RT\)
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 2]
[ANSWER: C]
For the same operators \(N\) and \(a\) as above, what is \([N,a^2+3a+2I]\)?

(A) \(-a^2-3a\)
(B) \(-2a^2+3a\)
(C) \(-2a^2-3a\)
(D) \(2a^2+3a\)
(E) \(-2a^2-3a+2I\)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Global Phase, Relative Phase, and Interference
nodes.explanation: Distinguish a physically irrelevant overall phase from a relative phase that changes measurement probabilities. Use normalized two-component states and an explicitly supplied recombination matrix to predict interference, introducing Euler's formula as needed. Assume the calibrated Born-rule calculation and complex arithmetic, with no optics background. Do not infer an observable trajectory from interference or introduce time evolution yet.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: The same component probabilities can hide a difference ===
A preparation produces the normalized two-component state \(\boldsymbol{\psi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Another produces \(\boldsymbol{\eta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix}\). Measuring which of the two original channels occurs gives probability \(1/2\) for each channel in either case. Can a device that combines the components distinguish the preparations?

Write a general state as \(\boldsymbol{\psi}=\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}\), where the complex amplitudes obey \(\lvert a\rvert^2+\lvert b\rvert^2=1\). The original-channel probabilities are \(P(0)=\lvert a\rvert^2\) and \(P(1)=\lvert b\rvert^2\). Their labels, \(0\) and \(1\), identify outcomes; they do not describe a particle's position or route.

A complex number has a magnitude and, when it is nonzero, an angle called its phase. Euler's formula writes a complex number of magnitude one as
\[
e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta.
\]
The real angle \(\theta\) is measured in radians. The right side has real part \(\cos\theta\), imaginary part \(\sin\theta\), and squared magnitude \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\). Multiplying an amplitude by \(e^{i\theta}\) therefore changes its phase without changing its magnitude.

[GRAPH]
type: parametric2d
title: A phase factor lies on the unit circle
xlabel: Real part
ylabel: Imaginary part
trange: 0, 6.283185307179586
xrange: -1.25, 1.25
yrange: -1.25, 1.25
trace: cos(t), sin(t) | label: Unit circle
segment: 0, 0, cos(s), sin(s) | label: Phase factor
point: cos(s), sin(s) | label: Tip
slider: s | range: -3.141592653589793, 3.141592653589793 | init: 0.7853981633974483 | step: 0.05
[/GRAPH]

The segment shows the complex number \(e^{is}\). Changing the slider changes its angle while its length remains one. This is a diagram of a complex amplitude, not an observable trajectory.

For example, \(e^{i\pi/2}=i\) and \(e^{i\pi}=-1\). Phases that differ by \(2\pi\) give the same complex number. Phase factors multiply by adding their angles: \(e^{i\alpha}e^{i\beta}=e^{i(\alpha+\beta)}\). These facts let us keep track of phase changes without repeatedly expanding every product into real and imaginary parts.

=== SECTION 2: Overall phase and the difference between component phases ===
Suppose the same phase factor multiplies every component:
\[
\boldsymbol{\psi}'=e^{i\chi}\boldsymbol{\psi}
=\begin{pmatrix}e^{i\chi}a\\e^{i\chi}b\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here \(\chi\) is an overall, or global, phase. Both original-channel probabilities stay the same because \(\lvert e^{i\chi}\rvert=1\).

The irrelevance of global phase goes beyond this particular measurement. If a measurement arrangement first combines amplitudes linearly through a matrix \(M\), then
\[
M\boldsymbol{\psi}'=M(e^{i\chi}\boldsymbol{\psi})=e^{i\chi}M\boldsymbol{\psi}.
\]
Every output amplitude receives the same factor of magnitude one, so every output probability stays the same. States differing only by global phase represent the same physical state.

For example, \(\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{3}/2\\1/2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}i\sqrt{3}/2\\i/2\end{pmatrix}\) differ by the single common factor \(i\). There is no measurement distinction caused by that factor.

A relative phase compares the phases of two nonzero components. If their phases are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), the phase of the second relative to the first is \(\phi=\beta-\alpha\), with angles understood modulo \(2\pi\). A common addition to both phases cancels in this difference. Changing only one component's phase generally changes the relative phase.

For instance,
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}e^{i\pi/4}\\2e^{-i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}
=e^{i\pi/4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2i\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Removing the global factor makes the first component real and positive. The second component then has phase \(-\pi/2\) relative to the first. Their unequal magnitudes do not affect that phase difference. If a component is zero, assigning it an angle has no physical effect, so a relative phase involving that zero component is not meaningful.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: A]
Which state differs from \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}i\\2\end{pmatrix}\) only by a global phase?

(A) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2i\end{pmatrix}\)
(B) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\2i\end{pmatrix}\)
(C) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}i\\-2\end{pmatrix}\)
(D) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\)
(E) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{pmatrix}2\\i\end{pmatrix}\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: Recombining amplitudes before measuring ===
Consider a device specified completely by the recombination matrix
\[
R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The input components refer to the original channels. After recombination, the components of \(R\boldsymbol{\psi}\) are the amplitudes for the two output channels. This matrix is a supplied rule for the device; no background about its construction is needed.

Matrix multiplication gives
\[
R\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}(a+b)/\sqrt{2}\\(a-b)/\sqrt{2}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first output receives a sum of amplitudes; the second receives a difference. We take squared magnitudes after those combinations. Thus
\[
P_R(0)=\frac{\lvert a+b\rvert^2}{2},\qquad
P_R(1)=\frac{\lvert a-b\rvert^2}{2}.
\]
The subscript identifies probabilities measured after this particular recombination. The identity \(\lvert a+b\rvert^2+\lvert a-b\rvert^2=2(\lvert a\rvert^2+\lvert b\rvert^2)\) ensures that the output probabilities add to one for every normalized input.

For the first preparation in the opening situation,
\[
R\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The matching input amplitudes reinforce in the first output and cancel in the second. The output probabilities are \(1\) and \(0\).

For the other preparation,
\[
R\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1+i\\1-i\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Since \(\lvert1+i\rvert^2=\lvert1-i\rvert^2=2\), its output probabilities are \(1/2\) and \(1/2\). Recombination distinguishes preparations whose original-channel probabilities were identical. Interference is this dependence of a combined probability on how amplitudes reinforce or cancel. Adding the original-channel probabilities would discard the phase information that controls it.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: D]
The input to the specified device is \(\frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}3\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). What are \(\bigl(P_R(0),P_R(1)\bigr)\)?

(A) \(\left(\frac{9}{25},\frac{16}{25}\right)\)
(B) \(\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right)\)
(C) \(\left(\frac{49}{50},\frac{1}{50}\right)\)
(D) \(\left(\frac{1}{50},\frac{49}{50}\right)\)
(E) \(\left(\frac{1}{10},\frac{9}{10}\right)\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: Predicting the interference pattern ===
For equal component magnitudes, we can remove an irrelevant global phase and write the input as
\[
\boldsymbol{\psi}_{\phi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\e^{i\phi}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here \(\phi\) is the relative phase. The normalization follows from the unit magnitude of \(e^{i\phi}\). The original-channel probabilities remain \(1/2\) and \(1/2\) for every \(\phi\).

The recombination matrix produces output amplitudes \((1+e^{i\phi})/2\) and \((1-e^{i\phi})/2\). Euler's formula makes their squared magnitudes manageable:
\[
\lvert1+e^{i\phi}\rvert^2=(1+\cos\phi)^2+\sin^2\phi=2+2\cos\phi,
\]
\[
\lvert1-e^{i\phi}\rvert^2=(1-\cos\phi)^2+\sin^2\phi=2-2\cos\phi.
\]
Consequently,
\[
P_R(0)=\frac{1+\cos\phi}{2},\qquad
P_R(1)=\frac{1-\cos\phi}{2}.
\]

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: Output probabilities as relative phase changes
xlabel: \(\phi\)
ylabel: Probability
xrange: 0, 6.283185307179586
yrange: -0.05, 1.05
trace: (1 + cos(x))/2 | label: \(P_R(0)\)
trace: (1 - cos(x))/2 | label: \(P_R(1)\)
point: 0, 1 | label: Reinforcement
point: 3.141592653589793, 0 | label: Cancellation
[/GRAPH]

The curves describe a family of preparations with different fixed relative phases. The horizontal axis is a phase angle, not elapsed time. At \(\phi=0\), the first output is fully reinforced. At \(\phi=\pi\), that output cancels completely. Probability shifts between outputs while their sum remains one. These extreme outcomes rely on the equal input magnitudes used in this family; the general matrix calculation still applies when the magnitudes differ.

For a worked intermediate case, take \(\phi=\pi/4\). Since \(\cos(\pi/4)=1/\sqrt{2}\), the output probabilities are \((2+\sqrt{2})/4\) and \((2-\sqrt{2})/4\). Relative phase can change output probabilities continuously, even though it leaves the original-channel probabilities unchanged.

A relative phase need not be distinguished by every measurement. This device's probabilities depend on \(\cos\phi\), and \(\cos(-\phi)=\cos\phi\). For example, the preparations with relative phases \(\pi/4\) and \(-\pi/4\) give the same output probabilities here. Their first components are identical and nonzero, so a common factor mapping one state to the other would have to be one; their second components differ. They are therefore distinct states despite agreeing on this measurement. Identical results from a particular measurement do not by themselves establish equivalence by global phase.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: A]
A preparation starts in \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\e^{i\pi/6}\end{pmatrix}\). A device multiplies only its second component by \(e^{i\pi/2}\), and the resulting state enters the specified recombination device. What is the probability of output channel \(0\)?

(A) \(\frac{1}{4}\)
(B) \(\frac{3}{4}\)
(C) \(\frac{1}{2}\)
(D) \(\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{4}\)
(E) \(\frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{4}\)
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: C]
An input is known to have the form \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\e^{i\phi}\end{pmatrix}\), with \(0\leq\phi<2\pi\). Repeated measurements after the specified recombination establish probabilities \(3/4\) and \(1/4\) for output channels \(0\) and \(1\). Which list contains all relative phases consistent with these probabilities?

(A) Only \(\pi/3\)
(B) \(\pi/3\) and \(4\pi/3\)
(C) \(\pi/3\) and \(5\pi/3\)
(D) \(2\pi/3\) and \(4\pi/3\)
(E) Every phase in the stated interval
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 2]
[ANSWER: B]
For any real \(\alpha\), an input to the specified recombination device is \(\frac{e^{i\alpha}}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\3i\end{pmatrix}\). What is the probability of output channel \(0\)?

(A) \(\frac{1}{10}\)
(B) \(\frac{1}{2}\)
(C) \(\frac{9}{10}\)
(D) \(\frac{1+\cos\alpha}{2}\)
(E) \(\frac{1+\sin\alpha}{2}\)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Fourier Transforms and Wave Packets
nodes.explanation: Resolve a localized function into complex plane waves and reconstruct it using a consistent Fourier-transform convention. Work through a rectangular spectral amplitude and its spatial profile, introducing complex exponentials, inverse transforms, and norm preservation at a usable level. Assume the calibrated single-variable differentiation and integration; supply any additional integral identity. Interpret reciprocal widths without yet identifying wave number with momentum or proving quantum uncertainty.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: WAVES THAT EXTEND EVERYWHERE ===

A localized pulse is concentrated in a small region, while a sine or cosine wave extends indefinitely. How can extended waves build a localized function? Their contributions can reinforce near one location and cancel at others. A Fourier transform describes the weights needed for that combination.

A compact way to keep track of two oscillating components is a complex exponential. The imaginary unit \(i\) satisfies \(i^2=-1\), and Euler's identity states
\[
e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta.
\]
The angle \(\theta\) is real and measured in radians. The real part is \(\cos\theta\), and the imaginary part is \(\sin\theta\). For a complex number \(u+iv\), its squared magnitude is
\[
\lvert u+iv\rvert^2=u^2+v^2.
\]
Consequently \(\lvert e^{i\theta}\rvert=1\), even though its two components oscillate.

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: The two components of a complex exponential
xlabel: \(\theta\)
ylabel: component
xrange: -6.283185307, 6.283185307
yrange: -1.2, 1.2
trace: cos(x) | label: Real part, \(\cos\theta\)
trace: sin(x) | label: Imaginary part, \(\sin\theta\)
[/GRAPH]

For a spatial coordinate \(x\), the function \(e^{ikx}\) is a complex plane wave. The real number \(k\), called the wave number, determines how rapidly its phase \(kx\) changes with position. The product \(kx\) is dimensionless, so \(k\) has units of inverse length when \(x\) has units of length. For \(k\ne0\), the spatial period is \(2\pi/\lvert k\rvert\). There is no time variable in this expression.

Changing the sign of the phase reverses the imaginary component:
\[
e^{-i\theta}=\cos\theta-i\sin\theta.
\]
For example, adding two opposite wave numbers gives
\[
e^{2ix}+e^{-2ix}=2\cos(2x).
\]
The imaginary components cancel. A combination of complex waves can therefore produce a real function.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: D]
What are the real and imaginary parts of \(e^{-2ix}\) at \(x=\pi/6\), in that order?

(A) \(1/2,\ \sqrt{3}/2\)
(B) \(\sqrt{3}/2,\ -1/2\)
(C) \(-1/2,\ -\sqrt{3}/2\)
(D) \(1/2,\ -\sqrt{3}/2\)
(E) \(-1/2,\ \sqrt{3}/2\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: COEFFICIENTS AND RECONSTRUCTION ===

Let \(f(x)\) be the function we want to describe, and let \(F(k)\) give its spectral amplitude: the complex weight assigned to each wave number. We will use one convention consistently:
\[
F(k)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)e^{-ikx}\,dx,
\]
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}F(k)e^{ikx}\,dk.
\]
The first equation is the forward transform; it finds the spectral amplitudes. The second is the inverse transform; it reconstructs the spatial function by adding the weighted plane waves. Its integration variable is \(k\), while \(x\) is held fixed. An integral of a complex function means integrating its real and imaginary parts separately.

The opposite signs in the two exponentials and the matching factors \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\) belong together. Other conventions exist, but factors from different conventions cannot be mixed. These formulas apply directly when the integrals converge and have a standard limiting interpretation for finite-norm packets when an integral is not absolutely convergent.

A single plane wave has constant magnitude and is not localized. The weights and relative phases in \(F(k)\) determine where the reconstructed contributions add and where they cancel.

The squared norm of a function is its integrated squared magnitude:
\[
\lVert f\rVert^2=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\lvert f(x)\rvert^2\,dx.
\]
A finite-norm function has a finite value of this integral. Calling a function normalized means that this squared norm equals \(1\).

For the convention above, Fourier transformation preserves the squared norm. We will use the following identity without proving it:
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\lvert f(x)\rvert^2\,dx
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\lvert F(k)\rvert^2\,dk.
\]
This is an equality of total integrals, not an equality between pointwise values at a position and a wave number. It lets us normalize a packet in whichever representation is simpler. Multiplying a function by a constant \(c\) multiplies its squared norm by \(\lvert c\rvert^2\).

=== SECTION 3: A RECTANGULAR SPECTRUM ===

Consider a spectrum that gives equal real amplitude to all wave numbers in a symmetric interval and zero amplitude outside it. Write its half-width as \(K>0\) and its positive amplitude as \(A\):
\[
F(k)=\begin{cases}
A,&-K\le k\le K,\\
0,&\lvert k\rvert>K.
\end{cases}
\]
Its full spectral width is \(2K\). Changing the value at an isolated endpoint does not affect any integral here.

Norm preservation makes the normalization particularly simple:
\[
\lVert f\rVert^2=\int_{-K}^{K}A^2\,dk=2KA^2.
\]
Thus the normalized rectangular spectrum has
\[
A=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2K}}.
\]
A wider normalized rectangle must be lower: its squared amplitude, multiplied by its width, stays equal to \(1\).

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: A normalized rectangular spectral amplitude
xlabel: \(k\)
ylabel: \(F(k)\)
xrange: -4, 4
yrange: -0.08, 1.12
trace: 0 | label: Zero reference | color: #A0A0A0
segment: -4, 0, -K, 0 | color: #147D92
segment: -K, 1/sqrt(2*K), K, 1/sqrt(2*K) | color: #147D92
segment: K, 0, 4, 0 | color: #147D92
segment: -K, 0, -K, 1/sqrt(2*K) | dashed: true | color: #A0A0A0
segment: K, 0, K, 1/sqrt(2*K) | dashed: true | color: #A0A0A0
slider: K | range: 0.5, 3 | init: 1 | step: 0.1
[/GRAPH]

The colored horizontal pieces represent the spectral amplitude. The zero reference and dashed vertical guides locate the rectangle; the vertical guides do not assign a range of amplitudes at its jumps. Move the half-width slider to see the normalized height change.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: A]
A spectrum is \(B\) for \(-2\le k<1\), \(2B\) for \(1\le k\le2\), and zero elsewhere, where \(B>0\). What value of \(B\) makes its reconstructed spatial function normalized?

(A) \(1/\sqrt{7}\)
(B) \(1/\sqrt{5}\)
(C) \(1/7\)
(D) \(1/\sqrt{3}\)
(E) \(\sqrt{2\pi/7}\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: THE PACKET IN SPACE ===

Return to the rectangular spectrum with amplitude \(A\) and half-width \(K\). The inverse transform reduces to a finite integral:
\[
f(x)=\frac{A}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-K}^{K}e^{ikx}\,dk.
\]
