=== SECTION 4: RETAINING TWO RECORDED BRANCHES ===

Keeping both outputs is a different accounting problem from keeping one. Suppose an incoming \(\lvert x+\rangle\) beam is measured along \(z\). We record the channel labels and retain both beams as distinguishable branches. Each branch then enters its own analyzer measuring \(S_x\).

The first measurement produces \(\lvert z+\rangle\) and \(\lvert z-\rangle\) with probabilities \(1/2\) each. Within either branch, the later plus probability along \(x\) is \(1/2\). The two mutually exclusive contributions to the final plus count therefore give
\[
p(\text{final }x+)=\frac12\frac12+\frac12\frac12=\frac12.
\]
If the original \(\lvert x+\rangle\) state were sent directly into an analyzer measuring \(S_x\), its plus probability would be \(1\). The intervening recorded measurement prepares a different ensemble for that final analyzer.

[GRAPH]
type: parametric2d
title: Two distinguishable branches contribute separate probabilities
xlabel: downstream distance
ylabel: channel position
trange: 0, 1
xrange: 0, 4.5
yrange: -1.8, 1.8
trace: t, 0 | label: Incoming \(\lvert x+\rangle\) | color: #606060
point: 1, 0 | label: \(S_z\)
segment: 1, 0, 2, 1 | label: \(z+\) | color: #147D92
segment: 1, 0, 2, -1 | label: \(z-\) | color: #AC6141
segment: 2, 1, 3, 1 | color: #147D92
segment: 2, -1, 3, -1 | color: #AC6141
point: 3, 1 | label: \(S_x\)
point: 3, -1 | label: \(S_x\)
segment: 3, 1, 4, 1.4 | label: \(x+\) | color: #147D92
segment: 3, 1, 4, 0.6 | label: \(x-\) | color: #147D92
segment: 3, -1, 4, -0.6 | label: \(x+\) | color: #AC6141
segment: 3, -1, 4, -1.4 | label: \(x-\) | color: #AC6141
[/GRAPH]

Add probabilities over the recorded, distinguishable branches. Coherently recombining amplitudes would require preserving their relative phases and bringing the paths together in a different apparatus. Counting the separate output channels does not perform such a recombination.

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: B]
An incoming \(\lvert y+\rangle\) beam is measured along \(x\). Both recorded outputs are retained as distinguishable branches. Each branch passes through a filter keeping only the plus outcome along \(z\), followed by a filter keeping only the plus outcome along \(y\). What fraction of the original beam passes the complete arrangement, counting both branches?

(A) \(1/8\)
(B) \(1/4\)
(C) \(1/2\)
(D) \(1\)
(E) \(0\)
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: C]
Particles begin in \(\lvert x+\rangle\). Sequence A keeps the minus output along \(y\), then the minus output along \(x\). Sequence B uses those same two filters in the reverse order. What are the transmission probabilities from the original beam for sequences A and B, in that order?

(A) \(0,\ 1/4\)
(B) \(1/2,\ 0\)
(C) \(1/4,\ 0\)
(D) \(1/4,\ 1/4\)
(E) \(0,\ 0\)
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 2]
[ANSWER: D]
Particles begin in \(\lvert z-\rangle\) and pass through three filters that keep, in order, the plus output along \(x\), the plus output along \(x\) again, and the minus output along \(y\). What fraction of the original beam passes all three?

(A) \(1/8\)
(B) \(1/2\)
(C) \(0\)
(D) \(1/4\)
(E) \(1\)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Spin Precession in a Constant Magnetic Field
nodes.explanation: Use H=−γ S·B to evolve a spin-one-half state in a uniform, constant magnetic field and calculate the time-dependent spin probabilities. Define the magnetic moment, gyromagnetic ratio, and field components needed by this model. Explain precession as changing relative phase rather than changing the probabilities in the energy basis. Oscillating fields and resonant driving are outside this lesson.

nodes.label: Angular Momentum as a Rotation Generator
nodes.explanation: Construct infinitesimal Cartesian rotations and use their noncommutativity to motivate [J_i,J_j]=iℏε_ijkJ_k. Define the index notation and required three-dimensional vector operations rather than assuming classical rigid-body mechanics. Show that J² commutes with each component while different components generally cannot have sharp values together. Establish the rotation algebra here; its allowed spectra are the next task.

nodes.label: Angular-Momentum Ladder Operators
nodes.explanation: Use J± and positivity of state norms to derive the joint J²,J_z eigenvalues and the allowed j,m ladders. Calculate normalized raising and lowering coefficients and construct a small-j operator representation. Distinguish integer and half-integer representations without assuming that every angular momentum is orbital. Coordinate eigenfunctions and addition of independent angular momenta require separate machinery.

nodes.label: The Three-Dimensional Schrödinger Equation
nodes.explanation: Build the scalar-potential Hamiltonian in three dimensions and apply the Cartesian or spherical Laplacian to a supplied wavefunction. Introduce gradients, partial derivatives in several variables, and the relevant Laplacian formulas explicitly, linking their use to the spherical volume element and normalization. Verify a simple separable solution without solving a new spectral problem. Angular eigenfunctions, central-potential separation, and electromagnetic vector potentials follow later.

nodes.label: Orbital Angular-Momentum Operators
nodes.explanation: Realize rotation generators as L=r×p acting on spatial wavefunctions and obtain usable expressions for L_z and L² in spherical coordinates. Define the cross product through its components and verify how these operators act on simple angular functions. Use single-valued spatial wavefunctions to explain the integer character of orbital angular momentum. Do not identify this restriction with the allowed intrinsic-spin representations; normalized spherical eigenfunctions come next.

nodes.label: Spherical Harmonics
nodes.explanation: Use Y_lm as the normalized joint eigenfunctions of orbital L² and L_z and interpret their angular probability distributions. Construct and normalize low-l examples, introducing the necessary Legendre-polynomial formulas and phase convention. Connect the coordinate functions to the abstract angular-momentum ladder coefficients. Focus on the angular basis and its orthogonality; radial dynamics and extensive special-function identities are excluded.

nodes.label: The Radial Schrödinger Equation for Central Potentials
nodes.explanation: Separate a rotationally invariant three-dimensional Hamiltonian into spherical harmonics and a radial equation. Use u(r)=rR(r) to obtain the effective one-dimensional equation with its centrifugal term, radial normalization, and origin boundary condition for regular potentials. Explain why the angular momentum changes radial motion even when the potential depends only on radius. Coulomb energy quantization and scattering asymptotics are subsequent applications.

nodes.label: Tensor Products of Quantum States and Operators
nodes.explanation: Build a joint Hilbert-space basis for two distinguishable systems, calculate product-state coefficients, and apply local operators such as A⊗I. Construct joint measurement projectors and distinguish a tensor product from an ordinary direct sum. Work with two finite systems so that the notation becomes computationally usable. Entanglement, particle indistinguishability, and reduced states are separate lessons rather than assumed meanings of the tensor product.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: A basis for pairs of outcomes ===

One system has two possible basis labels and a second has three. A joint description must distinguish every pair: knowing the first label does not tell us the second. How large is the space that can represent all these combinations?

Let system \( A \) have an orthonormal basis \( |a_j\rangle \), with \( j=1,\ldots,m \), and distinguishable system \( B \) have basis \( |b_k\rangle \), with \( k=1,\ldots,n \). Their joint space is the tensor product \( \mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal H_B \). Its basis vectors are

\[
|a_j\rangle\otimes|b_k\rangle.
\]

Read this as the vector with first-system label \( j \) and second-system label \( k \). We also write \( |a_j,b_k\rangle \). There are \( mn \) pairs. The inner product is defined so that

\[
\bigl(\langle a_j|\otimes\langle b_k|\bigr)
\bigl(|a_l\rangle\otimes|b_s\rangle\bigr)
=\langle a_j|a_l\rangle\langle b_k|b_s\rangle
=\delta_{jl}\delta_{ks}.
\]

The delta symbol is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. Thus the joint basis is orthonormal. A general joint vector is a linear combination of these basis vectors, with one complex coefficient for each pair.

For two two-dimensional systems, fix the ordered basis

\[
|00\rangle,\ |01\rangle,\ |10\rangle,\ |11\rangle,
\qquad |jk\rangle=|j\rangle_A\otimes|k\rangle_B.
\]

The second label changes fastest in this convention. Fixing an order matters because it determines which matrix row and column corresponds to each pair.

[TABLE]
Joint basis vector | First-system label | Second-system label
\( |00\rangle \) | \( 0 \) | \( 0 \)
\( |01\rangle \) | \( 0 \) | \( 1 \)
\( |10\rangle \) | \( 1 \) | \( 0 \)
\( |11\rangle \) | \( 1 \) | \( 1 \)
[/TABLE]

A direct sum \( \mathcal H_A\oplus\mathcal H_B \) has dimension \( m+n \). Its coordinate list concatenates a vector from one space and a vector from the other. It does not supply a basis entry for every joint pair. For two two-dimensional spaces the two dimensions happen to coincide, but the meanings and constructions still differ.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: C]
A distinguishable pair has component-space dimensions two and three. Which dimensions belong to its tensor product and the corresponding direct sum, in that order?

(A) \( 5,6 \)
(B) \( 5,5 \)
(C) \( 6,5 \)
(D) \( 6,6 \)
(E) \( 3,2 \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: Multiplying the coefficients ===

The tensor product is linear in either input. Therefore a product preparation expands by ordinary distribution:

\[
\bigl(a_0|0\rangle_A+a_1|1\rangle_A\bigr)
\otimes\bigl(b_0|0\rangle_B+b_1|1\rangle_B\bigr)
=\sum_{j,k=0}^1a_jb_k|jk\rangle.
\]

In the chosen order, its column is \( (a_0b_0,a_0b_1,a_1b_0,a_1b_1)^{\mathsf T} \). A coefficient multiplies another coefficient; their squared magnitudes are taken only when calculating probabilities.

For example, \( |a\rangle=(\sqrt3,i)^{\mathsf T}/2 \) and \( |b\rangle=(1,2)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5 \) give

\[
|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle
=\frac{1}{2\sqrt5}(\sqrt3,2\sqrt3,i,2i)^{\mathsf T}.
\]

The squared norm of a product is

\[
\sum_{j,k}|a_jb_k|^2
=\left(\sum_j|a_j|^2\right)\left(\sum_k|b_k|^2\right).
\]

Normalized component states therefore give a normalized product state. This is also the general identity \( \langle a\otimes b|a\otimes b\rangle=\langle a|a\rangle\langle b|b\rangle \).

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: D]
The two component states are \( (1,-i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \) and \( (2,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5 \). What is their product column in the specified joint basis?

(A) \( (2,-2i,1,-i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{10} \)
(B) \( (2,1,2i,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{10} \)
(C) \( (1,-i,2,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt7 \)
(D) \( (2,1,-2i,-i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{10} \)
(E) \( (4,1,4,1)^{\mathsf T}/10 \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: Operators that act on one component ===

For linear maps \( M \) on the first system and \( N \) on the second, define

\[
(M\otimes N)(|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle)
=(M|a\rangle)\otimes(N|b\rangle),
\]

and extend the action linearly to every joint vector. In particular, \( M\otimes I_B \) changes the first factor while the identity leaves the second factor unchanged.

In the chosen two-system basis, the matrix construction replaces each entry of \( M \) with that entry times the whole matrix \( N \):

\[
M\otimes N=\begin{pmatrix}M_{00}N&M_{01}N\\M_{10}N&M_{11}N\end{pmatrix}.
\]

These are matrix blocks. For example, \( M=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1) \) gives \( M\otimes I_B=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,-1,-1) \). The first two entries correspond to first label zero and the last two to first label one. This works for a general joint column, not only for a product preparation.

Products of such maps obey \( (M\otimes N)(R\otimes S)=MR\otimes NS \), as one can verify on every basis pair. Thus maps acting separately, \( M\otimes I_B \) and \( I_A\otimes N \), commute: both orders give \( M\otimes N \).

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: A]
Let \( X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} \), \( Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1) \), and \( |\psi\rangle=(1,i,2,0)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt6 \). What is \( (X\otimes Z)|\psi\rangle \)?

(A) \( (2,0,1,-i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt6 \)
(B) \( (i,1,0,-2)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt6 \)
(C) \( (2,0,-1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt6 \)
(D) \( (1,-i,2,0)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt6 \)
(E) \( (2,0,1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt6 \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: Joint and local measurement projectors ===

Suppose \( P_a \) selects an outcome of the first system and \( Q_b \) selects an outcome of the second. The joint projector is \( P_a\otimes Q_b \). It is Hermitian and idempotent because those properties hold in both factors. The projectors for all outcome pairs sum to \( I_A\otimes I_B \). The projective rule from Spectral Projectors and Projective Measurement therefore gives

\[
p(a,b)=\langle\psi|P_a\otimes Q_b|\psi\rangle.
\]

If only the first outcome is recorded, use \( P_a\otimes I_B \); summing over all second outcomes gives this projector by completeness. A nonzero-probability outcome has conditional joint state equal to its projected component divided by the square root of its probability.

For example, \( |\psi\rangle=(1,1,i,2)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt7 \). Recording second label one selects entries for \( |01\rangle \) and \( |11\rangle \), with projector \( \operatorname{diag}(0,1,0,1) \). The probability is \( 5/7 \), and the conditional joint state is \( (0,1,0,2)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5 \). Recording both labels would instead select a single entry for each pair.

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: B]
The joint input is \( (1,2,i,2i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{10} \). An ideal measurement records second-system label one. Which pair gives its probability and the conditional joint state?

(A) \( 1/2;\ (0,0,1,2)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5 \)
(B) \( 4/5;\ (0,1,0,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \)
(C) \( 2/5;\ (0,1,0,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \)
(D) \( 4/5;\ (0,2,0,2i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{10} \)
(E) \( 1/5;\ (1,0,i,0)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \)
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: E]
Let \( |+\rangle_A=(|0\rangle_A+|1\rangle_A)/\sqrt2 \). A joint measurement asks for first outcome \( |+\rangle_A \) and second outcome \( |1\rangle_B \). For input \( |0\rangle_A\otimes(|0\rangle_B+i|1\rangle_B)/\sqrt2 \), what is the probability of that joint outcome?

(A) \( 1 \)
(B) \( 1/2 \)
(C) \( 0 \)
(D) \( 1/8 \)
(E) \( 1/4 \)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Center-of-Mass and Relative Coordinates
nodes.explanation: Transform a two-particle Hamiltonian with an interaction V(|r₁−r₂|) into center-of-mass and relative-motion terms and derive the reduced mass. Work through the coordinate derivatives and explain when the wavefunction can separate. Supply the elementary mass-weighted mechanical interpretation rather than assuming a prior two-body mechanics course. This method reduces an interacting pair to an effective one-body problem; it does not remove exchange symmetry requirements.

nodes.label: Frobenius Series for Bound-State Equations
nodes.explanation: Find an admissible leading power near a regular singular point, substitute a power series, and derive the coefficient recurrence for a second-order differential equation. Teach index shifting and coefficient comparison explicitly through a simple supplied radial-type equation. Relate local regularity to the eventual need for a globally normalizable solution. Develop this new solution method here so the Coulomb problem need not conceal an unfamiliar special-functions technique.

nodes.label: Hydrogenic Energy Quantization
nodes.explanation: Apply radial asymptotics and a terminating Frobenius series to the attractive Coulomb potential and derive the hydrogenic bound-state energies and allowed n,l values. Introduce the charge, Coulomb constant, Bohr length, and reduced-mass energy scale used in the calculation. Explain degeneracy in the scalar Coulomb Hamiltonian. Focus on nonrelativistic energy quantization; normalized orbital distributions, spin effects, and relativistic corrections come later.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Orbitals and Radial Probability
nodes.explanation: Build low-lying normalized hydrogenic orbitals from their radial factors and spherical harmonics, and calculate angular or radial probabilities. Introduce the needed associated-Laguerre polynomial formulas and work through 1s and representative n=2 examples. Distinguish |ψ|² from r²|R|² and a probability maximum from a definite electron position. Use already-established quantum numbers and energies rather than repeating the spectrum derivation.

nodes.label: Nondegenerate First-Order Perturbation Theory
nodes.explanation: Expand the eigenvalue equation for H₀+λV and derive the first-order energy correction λ⟨n|V|n⟩. Apply it to a small matrix Hamiltonian and compare with the expansion of an exact eigenvalue to see what the approximation controls. Introduce H as the energy operator within the eigenvalue problem. Require an isolated unperturbed level; corrections to eigenvectors, second-order energies, and degenerate subspaces are separate tasks.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: Following an energy level when a matrix changes ===

Suppose a matrix has known eigenvalues, but a small extra interaction changes its entries. Solving the new characteristic equation exactly may be cumbersome. Can we predict the initial change of one energy level without solving the whole problem again?

The Hamiltonian \( H \) is the Hermitian operator representing energy. Its eigenvalues are the possible energy readouts. Consider the family

\[
H(\lambda)=H_0+\lambda V,
\]

where \( H_0 \) is the known Hamiltonian, \( V \) is a fixed Hermitian perturbation with units of energy, and \( \lambda \) is a dimensionless real parameter controlling its strength. This is a family of stationary eigenvalue problems, not a statement about how a state changes in time.

Choose a normalized eigenvector \( |n\rangle \) of \( H_0 \), with \( H_0|n\rangle=E_n^{(0)}|n\rangle \). Assume its eigenvalue is nondegenerate and separated from the other unperturbed energies by a nonzero gap. We follow the branch connected to this level for sufficiently small \( \lambda \), while it remains isolated.

Write its energy as

\[
E_n(\lambda)=E_n^{(0)}+\lambda E_n^{(1)}+O(\lambda^2).
\]

The superscripts label the unperturbed value and the coefficient of the first correction. The full first-order shift is \( \lambda E_n^{(1)} \), not \( E_n^{(1)} \) alone. The notation \( O(\lambda^2) \) means the omitted remainder is bounded in magnitude by a constant times \( \lambda^2 \) near zero, for this fixed isolated branch. It does not specify that constant or a numerical error at arbitrary strength.

=== SECTION 2: Deriving the energy correction ===

To expand the eigenvalue equation, allow the eigenvector to change as \( |\psi_n(\lambda)\rangle=|n\rangle+\lambda|\eta\rangle+O(\lambda^2) \). The auxiliary vector \( |\eta\rangle \) represents an unknown first-order change. We will not need to find it to obtain the energy coefficient.

Substitute both expansions into \( H(\lambda)|\psi_n(\lambda)\rangle=E_n(\lambda)|\psi_n(\lambda)\rangle \). The zeroth-order equation is the known unperturbed problem. Equating the coefficients of \( \lambda \) gives

\[
H_0|\eta\rangle+V|n\rangle
=E_n^{(0)}|\eta\rangle+E_n^{(1)}|n\rangle.
\]

Multiply from the left by \( \langle n| \). Since \( H_0 \) is Hermitian, \( \langle n|H_0=E_n^{(0)}\langle n| \). The two terms involving \( |\eta\rangle \) cancel. Normalization gives \( \langle n|n\rangle=1 \), leaving

\[
E_n^{(1)}=\langle n|V|n\rangle,\qquad
E_n(\lambda)\approx E_n^{(0)}+\lambda\langle n|V|n\rangle.
\]

Thus the initial energy slope is the perturbation's expectation in the unperturbed eigenstate, a matrix-element calculation already available from Quantum Expectation Values and Variances. It is real because the perturbation is Hermitian. The derivation did not assume the eigenvector stayed fixed; it showed why its unknown change cancels out of this projected equation.

For example, let \( H_0=\varepsilon\operatorname{diag}(0,4) \) and \( V=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} \), where \( \varepsilon>0 \) is a fixed energy unit. The lower unperturbed state is \( (1,0)^{\mathsf T} \). Its perturbation expectation is \( \varepsilon \), so the first-order estimate is \( E_-(\lambda)\approx\lambda\varepsilon \). The upper state's expectation is zero, so its estimate is \( E_+(\lambda)\approx4\varepsilon \).

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: C]
Let \( H_0=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} \) and \( V=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}3&i\\-i&1\end{pmatrix} \). For the level whose normalized unperturbed eigenvector is \( (1,-1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \), what is the first-order energy estimate?

(A) \( \varepsilon(3+2\lambda) \)
(B) \( \varepsilon(1+\lambda) \)
(C) \( \varepsilon(1+2\lambda) \)
(D) \( \varepsilon(1+2i\lambda) \)
(E) \( \varepsilon(1+4\lambda) \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: What comparison with an exact energy tells us ===

For the diagonal unperturbed example in the preceding section, the complete matrix is \( H(\lambda)=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&\lambda\\\lambda&4\end{pmatrix} \). Solving its two-dimensional characteristic equation gives

\[
E_\pm(\lambda)=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\left(4+\lambda\pm\sqrt{(4-\lambda)^2+4\lambda^2}\right).
\]

The minus branch connects to zero and the plus branch to \( 4\varepsilon \). To compare the initial slope, expand the square root at zero. Its value is four and its derivative is minus one, so it equals \( 4-\lambda+O(\lambda^2) \). Substitution yields \( E_-(\lambda)=\lambda\varepsilon+O(\lambda^2) \) and \( E_+(\lambda)=4\varepsilon+O(\lambda^2) \). This confirms precisely the constant and linear terms predicted above.

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: Exact lower energy and its first-order estimate
xlabel: \( \lambda \)
ylabel: \( E/\varepsilon \)
xrange: -0.8, 0.8
trace: (4+x-sqrt((4-x)^2+4*x^2))/2 | label: Exact lower branch
trace: x | label: First-order estimate
point: 0, 0 | label: Unperturbed level
[/GRAPH]

The curves have the same value and slope at zero. They need not agree farther away. At \( \lambda=0.1 \), the exact lower energy is approximately \( 0.097438\varepsilon \), compared with \( 0.1\varepsilon \) from first order. At \( \lambda=0.2 \), the exact value is approximately \( 0.189503\varepsilon \), compared with \( 0.2\varepsilon \). The increasing discrepancy is a remainder of the approximation, not a failure to include normalization in the matrix element.

Off-diagonal entries of the perturbation do not appear in its expectation for a single coordinate eigenvector. That fact does not make them irrelevant to the exact eigenvalues. Similarly, a zero first-order coefficient guarantees zero initial slope, not a constant exact energy.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: A]
For \( H(\lambda)=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}0&\lambda\\\lambda&3\end{pmatrix} \), consider the branch connected to zero. Its exact value is \( E_-(\lambda)=\varepsilon(3-\sqrt{9+4\lambda^2})/2 \). Which statement correctly compares it with first order?

(A) First order gives zero; the exact value is negative for nonzero \( \lambda \), which is consistent with an omitted remainder of order \( \lambda^2 \).
(B) First order gives \( \lambda\varepsilon \), because the off-diagonal entry is \( \lambda\varepsilon \).
(C) First order gives zero, so the exact energy must be zero at every strength.
(D) First order gives \( 3\varepsilon \), because the other unperturbed energy sets the correction.
(E) The exact formula disproves first order because it is not identically its linear estimate.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: The isolation assumption has a role ===

The estimate follows one particular level from the unperturbed problem. A small numerical value of \( \lambda \) alone does not make the physical perturbation small: the entries of \( V \) and the energy gaps also matter. Couplings comparable to a nearby level separation can strongly change the eigenvectors and spoil a first-order energy estimate. The derivation provides a local expansion, not a promise of accuracy after a level ceases to be isolated.

An exactly degenerate starting energy does not specify a unique vector \( |n\rangle \). Different normalized vectors in that eigenspace can give different expectations of \( V \); applying this isolated-level prescription to an arbitrary choice does not identify the actual energy branches. Our result assumes that ambiguity is absent.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: D]
An isolated branch has the expansion \( E(\lambda)=5\varepsilon-2\lambda\varepsilon+O(\lambda^2) \). Which conclusion is warranted?

(A) The exact energy is \( 5\varepsilon-2\lambda\varepsilon \) at every \( \lambda \).
(B) The error is exactly \( \lambda^2\varepsilon \).
(C) The eigenvector is independent of \( \lambda \).
(D) The energy's initial slope is \( -2\varepsilon \); the linear estimate alone does not give a numerical bound on its remainder at a specified nonzero strength.
(E) The remainder is necessarily negative.
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: B]
Let \( H_0=\varepsilon\operatorname{diag}(-1,2,6) \) and \( V=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}2&i&0\\-i&-3&4\\0&4&1\end{pmatrix} \). What are the first-order estimates for the branches starting at \( -\varepsilon \), \( 2\varepsilon \), and \( 6\varepsilon \), in that order?

(A) \( \varepsilon(-1+2\lambda),\varepsilon(2+3\lambda),\varepsilon(6+\lambda) \)
(B) \( \varepsilon(-1+2\lambda),\varepsilon(2-3\lambda),\varepsilon(6+\lambda) \)
(C) \( \varepsilon(-1+i\lambda),\varepsilon(2+4\lambda),6\varepsilon \)
(D) \( -\varepsilon,2\varepsilon,6\varepsilon \)
(E) \( 2\lambda\varepsilon,-3\lambda\varepsilon,\lambda\varepsilon \)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Perturbative State Mixing and Second-Order Energies
nodes.explanation: Calculate the first-order admixture of other unperturbed eigenstates and use it to obtain the second-order energy correction. Interpret matrix elements and energy denominators through a two-level example, estimating when mixing becomes too large for the expansion to be useful. Specify normalization to the working order. Connect the energy shift to virtual state mixing without introducing time-dependent transitions or applying the formula at degeneracy.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: How a perturbation changes the eigenvector ===
A perturbation can have zero diagonal matrix element and still change an energy level. For two unperturbed energies \(0\) and \(\Delta>0\), consider a coupling that gives
\[
H(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}0&\lambda g\\\lambda g&\Delta\end{pmatrix},\qquad g>0.
\]
The first-order energy correction of either level is zero. Nevertheless, the off-diagonal terms connect the two unperturbed basis states. Understanding the new eigenvectors will reveal the next energy correction.

Write the general Hamiltonian as \(H(\lambda)=H_0+\lambda V\), with real, dimensionless \(\lambda\) and Hermitian \(V\). Let \(H_0\lvert n\rangle=E_n^{(0)}\lvert n\rangle\), and assume the target level is isolated from the other unperturbed energies. Define \(V_{mn}=\langle m\rvert V\lvert n\rangle\); its units are energy.

Expand the eigenvalue and its eigenvector:
\[
E_n(\lambda)=E_n^{(0)}+\lambda E_n^{(1)}+\lambda^2E_n^{(2)}+O(\lambda^3),
\]
\[
\lvert\psi_n(\lambda)\rangle=\lvert n\rangle+\lambda\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle+\lambda^2\lvert n^{(2)}\rangle+O(\lambda^3).
\]
The superscripts label coefficients of the expansion. In particular, \(E_n^{(2)}\) is not the whole second-order contribution: that contribution is \(\lambda^2E_n^{(2)}\).

For the derivation near \(\lambda=0\), choose intermediate normalization, \(\langle n\mid\psi_n(\lambda)\rangle=1\). This fixes the coefficient along the original state and implies \(\langle n\mid n^{(1)}\rangle=\langle n\mid n^{(2)}\rangle=0\). It is a convenient choice of scale and phase for the eigenvalue equation, not a claim that the perturbed vector already has unit norm.

The coefficient of \(\lambda\) in the eigenvalue equation is
\[
H_0\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle+V\lvert n\rangle
=E_n^{(0)}\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle+E_n^{(1)}\lvert n\rangle.
\]
Projecting onto \(\langle n\rvert\) recovers \(E_n^{(1)}=V_{nn}\). For \(m\ne n\), projecting onto \(\langle m\rvert\) instead gives
\[
\bigl(E_m^{(0)}-E_n^{(0)}\bigr)\langle m\mid n^{(1)}\rangle=-V_{mn}.
\]
Hence
\[
\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle
=\sum_{m\ne n}\frac{V_{mn}}{E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}}\lvert m\rangle.
\]
The actual first-order admixture of \(\lvert m\rangle\) is \(\lambda V_{mn}/(E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)})\). Its phase comes from the matrix element and the signed denominator. Its size compares the coupling energy with the separation of the levels.

In the opening two-level example, the lower state has energy \(0\) and the other state has energy \(\Delta\). Its first-order correction is \(-g\lvert1\rangle/\Delta\). The intermediate-normalized lower eigenvector therefore begins as \(\lvert0\rangle-(\lambda g/\Delta)\lvert1\rangle\). The minus sign comes from the negative gap \(0-\Delta\).

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: A]
In the ordered unperturbed basis \(\lvert a\rangle,\lvert b\rangle,\lvert c\rangle\), let \(H_0=\varepsilon\operatorname{diag}(0,2,5)\) and \(V=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}0&2i&0\\-2i&1&3\\0&3&0\end{pmatrix}\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) is an energy unit. What is \(\lvert b^{(1)}\rangle\) in intermediate normalization?

(A) \(i\lvert a\rangle-\lvert c\rangle\)
(B) \(-i\lvert a\rangle-\lvert c\rangle\)
(C) \(i\lvert a\rangle+\lvert c\rangle\)
(D) \(2i\lvert a\rangle-3\lvert c\rangle\)
(E) \(\lvert b\rangle\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: Normalization at the working order ===
Let \(\lvert\chi\rangle=\lvert n\rangle+\lambda\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle\) be the first-order truncated vector. Orthogonality to \(\lvert n\rangle\) gives
\[
\langle\chi\mid\chi\rangle=1+\lambda^2S,\qquad
S=\langle n^{(1)}\mid n^{(1)}\rangle
=\sum_{m\ne n}\frac{\lvert V_{mn}\rvert^2}{\bigl(E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}\bigr)^2}.
\]
Intermediate normalization already preserves the norm through first order. At second order, the additional components contribute positive squared magnitudes and must be accounted for.

The exactly normalized version of this truncated vector is
\[
\lvert\chi_{\mathrm{norm}}\rangle
=\frac{\lvert n\rangle+\lambda\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle}{\sqrt{1+\lambda^2S}}.
\]
Expanding its normalization factor gives \((1+\lambda^2S)^{-1/2}=1-\lambda^2S/2+O(\lambda^4)\). Thus normalization supplies a correction \(-\lambda^2S\lvert n\rangle/2\) along the original state. This normalizes the truncation; it does not calculate the additional orthogonal terms in the full second-order eigenvector.

For example, \(\lvert0\rangle-0.1\lvert1\rangle\) has squared norm \(1.01\). Dividing by \(\sqrt{1.01}\) makes its probabilities in that unperturbed basis \(1/1.01\) and \(0.01/1.01\). A coefficient retained as one by intermediate normalization is not itself a probability of one.

The leading probability weight in another unperturbed state is \(\lambda^2\lvert V_{mn}/(E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)})\rvert^2\). These weights describe components of a perturbed eigenstate in the unperturbed basis. They do not describe a sequence of visits to other energy levels.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: A]
A calculation produces \(\lvert\chi\rangle=\lvert n\rangle+\frac{i}{5}\lvert a\rangle-\frac{1}{10}\lvert b\rangle\), with the three displayed basis states orthonormal. After normalizing this vector exactly, what is the probability of its \(\lvert n\rangle\) component?

(A) \(20/21\)
(B) \(19/20\)
(C) \(1\)
(D) \(25/26\)
(E) \(100/109\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: Mixing feeds back into the energy ===
Collecting the coefficient of \(\lambda^2\) in the eigenvalue equation gives
\[
H_0\lvert n^{(2)}\rangle+V\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle
=E_n^{(0)}\lvert n^{(2)}\rangle+E_n^{(1)}\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle+E_n^{(2)}\lvert n\rangle.
\]
Project onto \(\langle n\rvert\). The terms containing \(H_0\) and \(E_n^{(0)}\) cancel. The term containing \(E_n^{(1)}\) vanishes because intermediate normalization made \(\langle n\mid n^{(1)}\rangle=0\). Therefore
\[
E_n^{(2)}=\langle n\rvert V\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle
=\sum_{m\ne n}\frac{V_{nm}V_{mn}}{E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}}.
\]
Hermiticity means \(V_{nm}=V_{mn}^*\), so
\[
E_n^{(2)}=\sum_{m\ne n}\frac{\lvert V_{mn}\rvert^2}{E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}}.
\]
The numerator is a squared magnitude even when the coupling is complex. The denominator retains its sign. Each term has units of energy.

A coupled level above the target contributes negatively; one below the target contributes positively. For a nondegenerate lowest level, all these contributions are nonpositive. The opening two-level system gives
\[
E_0^{(2)}=-\frac{g^2}{\Delta},\qquad
E_1^{(2)}=\frac{g^2}{\Delta}.
\]
The lower energy moves down and the upper energy moves up by \(\lambda^2g^2/\Delta\) at this order. This separation is often called level repulsion.

The connection is visible directly in the derivation: the perturbation first supplies an admixture proportional to \(V_{mn}\), and projecting its effect back onto the original state supplies \(V_{nm}\). The phrase virtual mixing refers here to these contributions within a stationary eigenvalue calculation. It does not mean that the system actually undergoes two successive transitions.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: B]
A target level has unperturbed energy \(4\varepsilon\). The only other coupled levels have energies \(0\) and \(10\varepsilon\), with matrix elements \(\langle a\rvert V\lvert n\rangle=2\varepsilon\) and \(\langle c\rvert V\lvert n\rangle=3i\varepsilon\), respectively. At \(\lambda=1/5\), what is the second-order contribution to the target energy?

(A) \(-\varepsilon/2\)
(B) \(-\varepsilon/50\)
(C) \(\varepsilon/50\)
(D) \(\varepsilon/10\)
(E) \(-3\varepsilon/50\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: Exact two-level comparison and the size of mixing ===
The two-level Hamiltonian in the opening has exact eigenvalues
\[
E_\pm=\frac{\Delta\pm\sqrt{\Delta^2+4\lambda^2g^2}}{2}.
\]
The lower branch approaches \(0\) as \(\lambda\) approaches zero, and the upper branch approaches \(\Delta\). Define the dimensionless coupling-to-gap ratio \(a=\lambda g/\Delta\). Then
\[
\frac{E_-}{\Delta}=\frac{1-\sqrt{1+4a^2}}{2}.
\]
For small \(a\), the expansion \(\sqrt{1+x}=1+x/2+O(x^2)\) gives
\[
E_-=-\frac{\lambda^2g^2}{\Delta}+O(\Delta a^4),\qquad
E_+=\Delta+\frac{\lambda^2g^2}{\Delta}+O(\Delta a^4).
\]
This agrees with the second-order calculation. In this particular example the next energy term is fourth order because the exact energies depend only on \(\lambda^2\); a general perturbation can have a third-order term.

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: Exact and second-order lower energies
xlabel: \(a\)
ylabel: \(E_-/\Delta\)
xrange: 0, 0.8
yrange: -0.66, 0.02
trace: (1 - sqrt(1 + 4*x^2))/2 | label: Exact lower energy
trace: -(x^2) | label: Second-order lower energy
point: 0.6, (1 - sqrt(1 + 4*0.6^2))/2 | label: Exact
point: 0.6, -(0.6^2) | label: Approximate
segment: 0.6, -(0.6^2), 0.6, (1 - sqrt(1 + 4*0.6^2))/2 | label: Difference | dashed: true
[/GRAPH]

At \(a=0.1\), the exact scaled energy is about \(-0.009902\), compared with the second-order value \(-0.010000\). At \(a=0.6\), the values are about \(-0.2810\) and \(-0.3600\). The graph displays the increasing discrepancy; it does not establish a universal cutoff for accuracy.

The exact lower eigenvector, written with first component one, has second component
\[
r=-\frac{2a}{1+\sqrt{1+4a^2}}.
\]
This follows by substituting \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\r\end{pmatrix}\) into the eigenvalue equation: its first row gives \(\lambda g r=E_-\). The expression above is its continuous form at \(a=0\) as well. For small \(a\), it begins as \(r=-a+O(a^3)\), confirming the first-order admixture. Its unit-normalized column is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\r\end{pmatrix}/\sqrt{1+r^2}\).

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: Exact and first-order coefficient ratios
xlabel: \(a\)
ylabel: \(r\)
xrange: 0, 0.8
yrange: -0.82, 0.02
trace: -2*x/(1 + sqrt(1 + 4*x^2)) | label: Exact coefficient ratio
trace: -x | label: First-order coefficient ratio
point: 0.6, -2*0.6/(1 + sqrt(1 + 4*0.6^2)) | label: Exact
point: 0.6, -0.6 | label: First order
[/GRAPH]

At \(a=0.6\), the exact ratio is about \(-0.4684\), compared with the first-order value \(-0.6\). The first-order state also overestimates the amount of mixing in this case.

In a general system, inspect the ratios \(\eta_m=\lvert\lambda V_{mn}\rvert/\lvert E_n^{(0)}-E_m^{(0)}\rvert\). The squared norm of the first correction is \(\lambda^2S=\sum_{m\ne n}\eta_m^2\). If a ratio is comparable to one, or the sum is not small, the supposed correction is not small compared with the original state. A small numerical value of \(\lambda\) alone is insufficient. Small mixing supports the expansion when the perturbation also leaves the target level isolated; this is a practical estimate, not a general error bound.

At an exact unperturbed degeneracy, a denominator vanishes and the nondegenerate formula is inapplicable. Do not substitute a zero gap into it. Even before a gap reaches zero, the coupling-to-gap comparison can warn that this expansion is no longer useful.

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: A]
Two systems have the opening two-level form, both with \(\lambda=0.15\) and \(g=10\varepsilon\). Their gaps are \(\Delta_A=30\varepsilon\) and \(\Delta_B=\varepsilon\). Which assessment of the weak-mixing expansion is justified?

(A) The mixing ratios are \(0.05\) and \(1.5\); the expansion is reasonable for system A but uncontrolled for system B.
(B) The mixing ratios are \(1.5\) and \(0.05\); the expansion is reasonable for system B but uncontrolled for system A.
(C) Both are controlled because the numerical perturbation parameter is less than one.
(D) The mixing ratios are \(1/3\) and \(10\); neither system is in the small-mixing regime.
(E) System B gives the more reliable expansion because its unperturbed levels are closer.
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: A]
For real \(\theta\), let \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(0,\Delta)\) and \(V=\begin{pmatrix}0&g e^{-i\theta}\\g e^{i\theta}&0\end{pmatrix}\), with \(g,\Delta>0\). Which pair gives the leading admixture amplitude of \(\lvert1\rangle\) in the branch starting at \(\lvert0\rangle\), and its second-order energy contribution?

(A) \(-\lambda g e^{i\theta}/\Delta\) and \(-\lambda^2g^2/\Delta\)
(B) \(-\lambda g e^{-i\theta}/\Delta\) and \(-\lambda^2g^2/\Delta\)
(C) \(-\lambda g e^{i\theta}/\Delta\) and \(-\lambda^2g^2e^{2i\theta}/\Delta\)
(D) \(\lambda g e^{i\theta}/\Delta\) and \(\lambda^2g^2/\Delta\)
(E) \(-\lambda g/\Delta\) and \(-\lambda^2g^2\cos^2\theta/\Delta\)
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 2]
[ANSWER: D]
A target has unperturbed energy \(4\varepsilon\) and is coupled only to states at \(0\) and \(10\varepsilon\). Their matrix elements into the target column are \(2\varepsilon\) and \(i\sqrt{6}\,\varepsilon\), respectively. Which conclusion follows for \(E_n^{(2)}\) and \(\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle\)?

(A) \(E_n^{(2)}=2\varepsilon\), and \(\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle\ne0\).
(B) \(E_n^{(2)}=-2\varepsilon\), and \(\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle\ne0\).
(C) Both \(E_n^{(2)}\) and \(\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle\) vanish.
(D) \(E_n^{(2)}=0\), while \(\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle\ne0\).
(E) \(E_n^{(2)}=2i\varepsilon\), and \(\lvert n^{(1)}\rangle\ne0\).
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Degenerate Perturbation Theory
nodes.explanation: Project a perturbation into a degenerate eigenspace, diagonalize that restricted matrix, and identify the appropriate zeroth-order states and first-order splittings. Use a two-dimensional degenerate subspace to show why taking arbitrary diagonal expectations is insufficient. Separate mixing within the degenerate subspace from coupling to other energies. Limit the method to first order and leave near-degenerate resummation and second-order effective Hamiltonians outside the lesson.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: Equal unperturbed energies need a different starting basis ===

Two independent states can have the same unperturbed energy. A weak perturbation may separate their energies, even when its expectation value is identical in both of the original states. How can we find the states that actually separate?

Consider \(H(\lambda)=H_0+\lambda V\), where \(\lambda\) is a small real dimensionless parameter and both matrices are Hermitian. In numerical examples, all energy entries use one fixed energy unit. Take
\[
H_0=\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix},\qquad
V=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The original orthonormal states \(|1\rangle=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\) and \(|2\rangle=(0,1)^{\mathsf T}\) both have energy \(5\). Their perturbation expectations are both \(1\). Applying the isolated-level rule separately to these arbitrary states would suggest two identical first-order shifts of \(\lambda\).

But the perturbation also connects the states: \(V|1\rangle=|1\rangle+2|2\rangle\). The original vectors are not eigenvectors of the perturbed Hamiltonian. Instead, form
\[
|+\rangle=\frac{|1\rangle+|2\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad
|-\rangle=\frac{|1\rangle-|2\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
\]
Direct multiplication gives \(V|+\rangle=3|+\rangle\) and \(V|-\rangle=-|-\rangle\). Since \(H_0\) multiplies every vector here by \(5\), these combinations have energies \(5+3\lambda\) and \(5-\lambda\).

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: A perturbation splits a degenerate energy
xlabel: \(\lambda\)
ylabel: Energy in the chosen unit
xrange: 0, 0.3
yrange: 4.6, 6
trace: 5+3*x | label: Symmetric state
trace: 5-x | label: Antisymmetric state
point: 0, 5 | label: Degenerate energy
segment: 0.2, 4.8, 0.2, 5.6 | label: \(\Delta E=0.8\) | dashed: true
[/GRAPH]

For positive \(\lambda\), the separation is \(4\lambda\). The two straight lines are exact for this particular closed two-dimensional model. In a larger system, the same calculation within a degenerate eigenspace determines first-order energies, with additional corrections outside the present approximation.

Choosing different coordinates has not created a splitting. It has exposed the combinations on which the physical perturbation acts independently. Degeneracy permits these combinations because every linear combination within the original eigenspace still has the same unperturbed energy.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: B]
On a two-dimensional space, \(H_0=E_0I\) and \(V=\begin{pmatrix}0&3\\3&0\end{pmatrix}\) in the orthonormal basis \(|1\rangle,|2\rangle\). For nonzero \(\lambda\), which first-order description is correct?

(A) Both shifts vanish, with zeroth-order states \(|1\rangle\) and \(|2\rangle\).
(B) The shifts are \(+3\lambda\) and \(-3\lambda\), with states \((|1\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \((|1\rangle-|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\), respectively.
(C) The shifts are \(+3\lambda\) and \(-3\lambda\), with states \(|1\rangle\) and \(|2\rangle\), respectively.
(D) Both shifts are \(3\lambda\), with states \((|1\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \((|1\rangle-|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\).
(E) The shifts are \(+9\lambda\) and \(-9\lambda\), with states \((|1\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \((|1\rangle-|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\), respectively.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: Projecting the first-order eigenvalue equation ===

Let \(E_0\) now be a twofold-degenerate eigenvalue of a larger \(H_0\). Choose orthonormal vectors \(|1\rangle,|2\rangle\) spanning its eigenspace and define
\[
P=|1\rangle\langle1|+|2\rangle\langle2|.
\]
This projector keeps exactly the states with unperturbed energy \(E_0\). Seek a perturbed branch whose leading state is a normalized vector \(|u\rangle\) in that space:
\[
E(\lambda)=E_0+\lambda\varepsilon+O(\lambda^2),\qquad
|\psi(\lambda)\rangle=|u\rangle+\lambda|w\rangle+O(\lambda^2).
\]
The coefficient \(\varepsilon\) is the first-order energy coefficient; the energy shift is \(\lambda\varepsilon\). The vector \(|w\rangle\) is an unknown correction used here only to obtain the condition on \(|u\rangle\); we do not calculate it.

Substitute the expansions into the eigenvalue equation and collect the terms proportional to \(\lambda\):
\[
(H_0-E_0I)|w\rangle+V|u\rangle=\varepsilon|u\rangle.
\]
Project with \(P\). Since \(P(H_0-E_0I)=0\) and \(P|u\rangle=|u\rangle\), the unknown correction disappears:
\[
PVP|u\rangle=\varepsilon|u\rangle.
\]
Thus the appropriate zeroth-order states are eigenvectors of the perturbation restricted to the degenerate eigenspace.

In the chosen two-vector basis, the restricted matrix is
\[
W=\begin{pmatrix}
\langle1|V|1\rangle&\langle1|V|2\rangle\\
\langle2|V|1\rangle&\langle2|V|2\rangle
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It is Hermitian because \(V\) is Hermitian. Solve \(Wc=\varepsilon c\) with \(c^\dagger c=1\), then reconstruct \(|u\rangle=c_1|1\rangle+c_2|2\rangle\). Each eigenvalue supplies a branch \(E_0+\lambda\varepsilon+O(\lambda^2)\). The full-space matrix \(PVP\) also vanishes outside the chosen space; those outside zeros are not additional candidates for this degenerate level. We diagonalize its restriction \(W\).

For example,
\[
H_0=\operatorname{diag}(2,2,8),\qquad
V=\begin{pmatrix}1&-i&4\\i&1&2\\4&2&6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The degenerate space is spanned by the first two coordinate vectors, so
\[
P=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0),\qquad
PVP=\begin{pmatrix}1&-i&0\\i&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
W=\begin{pmatrix}1&-i\\i&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The restricted eigenvalues are \(0\) and \(2\). Their normalized leading states in the full space are \((1,-i,0)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\) and \((1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\). The associated energies are \(2+O(\lambda^2)\) and \(2+2\lambda+O(\lambda^2)\). The couplings to the third coordinate have been removed by projection rather than inserted into this first-order matrix.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: D]
Let \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(4,9,4)\) and \(V=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&i\\1&7&3\\-i&3&2\end{pmatrix}\). Which restricted matrix determines the first-order coefficients for the degenerate energy \(4\), in the ordered basis consisting of the first and third coordinate vectors?

(A) \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&7\end{pmatrix}\)
(B) \(\begin{pmatrix}2&-i\\i&2\end{pmatrix}\)
(C) \(\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\)
(D) \(\begin{pmatrix}2&i\\-i&2\end{pmatrix}\)
(E) \(\begin{pmatrix}7&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}\)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: The splitting is independent of the basis ===

The same degenerate eigenspace can be described by many orthonormal bases. If a unitary coordinate change within it is represented by \(U\), the restricted matrix changes to \(W'=U^\dagger WU\). These matrices have the same eigenvalues. Their eigenvector columns change coordinates, while the reconstructed physical vectors and the first-order energy branches agree.

Diagonal entries alone lack that invariance. They are perturbation expectations in the particular basis vectors chosen. They become first-order energy coefficients only when that basis diagonalizes the restricted perturbation. The task is to identify its eigenvalues and eigendirections, rather than assign physical meaning to arbitrary diagonal entries.

For a general two-dimensional Hermitian restriction,
\[
W=\begin{pmatrix}a&z\\\overline z&b\end{pmatrix},
\qquad a,b\text{ real},
\]
the characteristic equation is \((a-\varepsilon)(b-\varepsilon)-|z|^2=0\). Its two coefficients are
\[
\varepsilon_\pm=\frac{a+b}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\frac{a-b}{2}\right)^2+|z|^2}.
\]
An off-diagonal coupling can therefore separate the coefficients even when the diagonal entries agree. The corresponding states still come from the eigenvector equations; the eigenvalue formula by itself does not identify which combination belongs to which branch.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: C]
In an orthonormal basis \(|1\rangle,|2\rangle\) of a degenerate energy-\(E_0\) space, the restricted perturbation is \(W=\begin{pmatrix}3&2i\\-2i&3\end{pmatrix}\). For positive \(\lambda\), which shifts and normalized leading state of the higher branch are correct?

(A) Both shifts are \(3\lambda\); the higher branch can be identified with \(|1\rangle\).
(B) The shifts are \(-2\lambda\) and \(2\lambda\); the higher state is \((i|1\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\).
(C) The shifts are \(\lambda\) and \(5\lambda\); the higher state is \((i|1\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\).
(D) The shifts are \(\lambda\) and \(5\lambda\); the higher state is \((-i|1\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\).
(E) The shifts are \(-5\lambda\) and \(5\lambda\); the higher state is \((|1\rangle+|2\rangle)/\sqrt2\).
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: What the first-order result does and does not determine ===

Mixing within the degenerate space is part of selecting the leading states. It need not be a small rotation: the combinations in the opening example remain equally weighted however small a nonzero positive \(\lambda\) becomes. There is no unperturbed energy cost for choosing a different direction inside that space.

Coupling to states with different unperturbed energies has a different role. It contributes to corrections to the full states, but it does not enter the projected first-order energy matrix. This does not mean the couplings vanish in the actual Hamiltonian or can be ignored for every purpose. It means that the first-order energy equation for this level has already isolated the part needed at this order.

The degenerate level should remain isolated from the other unperturbed energies on the perturbation scale. In a small matrix, compare \(|\lambda|\) times the matrix elements connecting the chosen space to other levels with the corresponding nonzero unperturbed energy gaps. The ratios should be small for this isolated-space first-order treatment. If those scales are comparable, the present approximation does not provide a controlled description of the resulting mixing. This scale comparison is a practical validity check, not a numerical error bound.

A further limit appears when \(W\) has repeated eigenvalues. In two dimensions, \(W=cI\) gives the same first-order shift \(\lambda c\) for both states. No splitting or preferred direction within that space is selected at first order. This conclusion does not establish exact degeneracy for the full Hamiltonian: terms beyond the stated order have not been determined.

Finally, a nonzero separation between the two eigenvalues of \(W\) produces a first-order separation \(|\lambda|\,|\varepsilon_+-\varepsilon_-|\). The physical branches are determined by the restricted perturbation, while changing the original orthonormal basis changes only their representation.

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: A]
Let \(H_0=\operatorname{diag}(0,0,12)\) and \(V=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&1\\0&2&3\\1&3&7\end{pmatrix}\). Assume \(\lambda\ne0\) is small enough for the energy-\(0\) subspace to remain isolated. What are the two first-order energy shifts originating from that subspace?

(A) \(2\lambda\) and \(2\lambda\)
(B) \(3\lambda\) and \(5\lambda\)
(C) \((2-\sqrt{10})\lambda\) and \((2+\sqrt{10})\lambda\)
(D) \(2\lambda\) and \(7\lambda\)
(E) \(0\) and \(0\)
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: E]
A twofold-degenerate energy \(E_0\) has restricted perturbation \(W=\begin{pmatrix}1&i\\-i&3\end{pmatrix}\). For nonzero \(\lambda\), what is the magnitude of the first-order separation between the two resulting energies?

(A) \(4|\lambda|\)
(B) \(2|\lambda|\)
(C) \(\sqrt2|\lambda|\)
(D) \(0\)
(E) \(2\sqrt2|\lambda|\)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: The Variational Principle
nodes.explanation: Prove that the normalized energy expectation of an admissible trial state bounds the ground-state energy from above, then optimize a one-parameter trial family. Use a small Hamiltonian first so that trial-state quality and normalization are visible. Explain why the result does not directly bound an arbitrary excited level and why an upper energy bound is not a pointwise wavefunction error bound. Finite-basis generalized eigenvalue methods follow separately.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: A useful energy without an exact ground state ===

Suppose the lowest eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian is unknown, but you can calculate an energy expectation in a guessed state. Can that number constrain the exact ground-state energy? The variational principle supplies a one-sided guarantee and a practical reason to improve the guess.

The Hamiltonian \( H \) is a Hermitian energy operator. In the finite examples here it has orthonormal eigenstates \( |n\rangle \) and eigenvalues ordered as \( E_0\leq E_1\leq\cdots \). A ground state belongs to the lowest-energy eigenspace. An admissible trial state is a nonzero vector on which the Hamiltonian and its energy expectation are defined. Every finite vector is admissible for a finite matrix; more general operators can impose additional domain conditions.

For a normalized trial state \( |\psi\rangle=\sum_n c_n|n\rangle \), completeness and orthogonality give

\[
E_{\rm trial}=\langle\psi|H|\psi\rangle=\sum_n|c_n|^2E_n,
\qquad \sum_n|c_n|^2=1.
\]

Subtract the lowest energy:

\[
E_{\rm trial}-E_0=\sum_n|c_n|^2(E_n-E_0)\geq0.
\]

Each summand is nonnegative. Therefore \( E_0\leq E_{\rm trial} \): the trial expectation is an upper bound. Equality holds exactly when the trial state lies entirely in the ground eigenspace. If the ground energy is degenerate, no particular vector within that eigenspace is singled out.

For an unnormalized trial vector \( |v\rangle \), the same expectation is the quotient

\[
E[v]=\frac{\langle v|H|v\rangle}{\langle v|v\rangle}.
\]

Its denominator removes arbitrary scale. Minimizing the numerator alone would not be a meaningful search: rescaling a vector changes that numerator without changing its direction.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: C]
Two admissible trial states for the same Hamiltonian give energies \( -2.1\varepsilon \) and \( -2.4\varepsilon \), where \( \varepsilon>0 \). Which conclusion follows without further information?

(A) \( E_0\geq-2.1\varepsilon \).
(B) \( E_0=-2.4\varepsilon \).
(C) \( E_0\leq-2.4\varepsilon \), and the second result is the tighter upper bound.
(D) \( -2.4\varepsilon\leq E_0\leq-2.1\varepsilon \).
(E) The first state has a smaller pointwise wavefunction error everywhere.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: Optimizing a one-parameter family ===

Take \( H=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&3\end{pmatrix} \) and trial vectors \( |v(t)\rangle=(1,t)^{\mathsf T} \), with real \( t\geq0 \). Their squared norm is \( 1+t^2 \). Matrix multiplication gives

\[
E(t)=\varepsilon\frac{1-2t+3t^2}{1+t^2}.
\]

The quotient converts the parameter into a genuine normalized energy expectation. Differentiating gives

\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=\frac{2\varepsilon(t^2+2t-1)}{(1+t^2)^2}.
\]

The allowed stationary point is \( t=\sqrt2-1 \). The derivative is negative before it and positive after it, so this is the minimum on the allowed interval. Substitution gives \( E_{\min}=(2-\sqrt2)\varepsilon \), improving the trial value \( E(0)=\varepsilon \).

[GRAPH]
type: function2d
title: Improving the trial energy by changing the coefficient ratio
xlabel: \( t \)
ylabel: \( E/\varepsilon \)
xrange: 0, 2
trace: (1-2*x+3*x^2)/(1+x^2) | label: Normalized trial energy
point: 0, 1 | label: Starting trial
point: sqrt(2)-1, 2-sqrt(2) | label: Minimum
[/GRAPH]

In this small example the exact eigenvalues are \( (2\pm\sqrt2)\varepsilon \), so the family contains an exact ground-state direction. In a restricted family that misses the ground eigenspace, optimization instead gives a strict upper bound. Enlarging the allowed family cannot raise its minimum because all the old choices remain available.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: B]
For \( H=\varepsilon\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix} \), consider trial vectors \( (1,t)^{\mathsf T} \) with \( t\geq0 \). Which parameter and minimized expectation are correct?

(A) \( t=0,\quad2\varepsilon \)
(B) \( t=1,\quad\varepsilon \)
(C) \( t=1,\quad2\varepsilon \)
(D) \( t=2,\quad0 \)
(E) \( t=1,\quad-\varepsilon \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: Why an excited level needs another constraint ===

The preceding proof uses the lowest energy among all states allowed in the trial search. An arbitrary trial vector may contain the ground state, so its expectation need not lie above a chosen excited energy. For example, for \( H=\varepsilon\operatorname{diag}(0,3) \), the normalized vector \( (1,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \) gives \( 3\varepsilon/2 \), below the excited energy \( 3\varepsilon \).

If a trial state is known to be orthogonal to every eigenstate below a target energy, those lower-energy weights vanish in the spectral expansion. The same nonnegative-sum argument then bounds that target from above. Without such a constraint, ground-state minimization does not automatically estimate an arbitrary excited level.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: D]
A nondegenerate Hamiltonian has eigenstates \( |0\rangle,|1\rangle,|2\rangle \) with increasing energies. A normalized trial state is orthogonal to \( |0\rangle \), with no further constraint. What bound is guaranteed?

(A) Its expectation is exactly \( E_1 \).
(B) Its expectation is at least \( E_2 \).
(C) Its expectation is at most \( E_1 \).
(D) Its expectation is at least \( E_1 \), but need not be at least \( E_2 \).
(E) No bound follows because the trial state need not be an eigenstate.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: Energy quality and state quality ===

An energy bound is a statement about one integrated or matrix expectation. It is not an error bound on every coordinate of a vector or every point of a spatial wavefunction. Degeneracy provides an immediate warning: different ground eigenvectors have the same exact energy.

Even without degeneracy, a small absolute energy error can coexist with substantial weight outside the ground direction when the gap is small. For \( H=\operatorname{diag}(0,0.002\varepsilon) \), the vector \( (1,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \) has energy \( 0.001\varepsilon \), yet half its squared norm lies in the excited direction. Energy error alone, without information about the spectrum, cannot certify a specified state accuracy.

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: A]
A normalized trial state has energy very close to the exact ground energy. Which conclusion is warranted from that fact alone?

(A) Its energy estimate is close, while a specified component-by-component or pointwise state accuracy needs additional information.
(B) Every coefficient differs from one chosen ground eigenvector by at most the energy error.
(C) It is exactly the ground state.
(D) Its energy lies below the ground energy.
(E) Its probability distribution must agree exactly with the ground-state distribution.
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: E]
For \( H=\varepsilon\operatorname{diag}(1,5) \), an unnormalized trial vector is \( (2,1)^{\mathsf T} \). What upper bound on the ground energy does this vector provide?

(A) \( 9\varepsilon \)
(B) \( 3\varepsilon \)
(C) \( 5\varepsilon/9 \)
(D) \( \varepsilon \)
(E) \( 9\varepsilon/5 \)
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: The Rayleigh–Ritz Method
nodes.explanation: Turn variational optimization over a finite trial subspace into a matrix eigenvalue problem and calculate an approximate ground energy. Include an explicitly computed overlap matrix for a small nonorthogonal basis and explain the generalized equation Hc=ESc. Compare nested subspaces to interpret systematic improvement without assuming prior numerical analysis. Leave rigorous excited-state minimax theorems and large-scale algorithms outside this lesson.

nodes.label: WKB Wavefunctions Away from Turning Points
nodes.explanation: Construct leading semiclassical wavefunctions in allowed and forbidden regions from the local momentum, including the inverse-square-root amplitude. Derive the slowly varying condition and interpret the allowed-region amplitude through probability flux. Use a smooth supplied potential to decide where the approximation is reliable. Do not extend it through a turning point or claim that a single local expression already quantizes the spectrum.

nodes.label: WKB Turning-Point Connection Formulas
nodes.explanation: Match oscillatory and exponential WKB solutions across a simple turning point by locally reducing the equation to the Airy form. Supply the Airy asymptotics and explain which coefficient and phase relations they imply rather than assuming special-function expertise. Practise connecting a decaying tail to the allowed-region solution. Restrict the formulas to smooth isolated linear turning points; hard walls and coalescing turning points require different treatment.

nodes.label: WKB Bound-State Quantization
nodes.explanation: Use two turning-point connections to derive and apply the semiclassical action quantization condition for a smooth confining well. Evaluate the action integral in an accessible example and interpret the half-integer offset as a boundary-phase effect. State the conditions under which the level estimate is reliable. Do not transfer the same offset uncritically to hard-wall or singular potentials.

nodes.label: WKB Tunneling Probabilities
nodes.explanation: Estimate transmission through a smooth forbidden region by integrating the imaginary local momentum between turning points. Connect the result to incoming and outgoing fluxes and compare its exponential dependence with the exact rectangular-barrier result. Distinguish a leading exponential estimate from a controlled prefactor calculation. Restrict the approximation to a sufficiently opaque barrier with well-separated simple turning points.

nodes.label: The Interaction Picture
nodes.explanation: Split H(t)=H₀+V(t), remove the known H₀ evolution, and derive the equation governed by V_I(t). Transform a two-level driving matrix explicitly to see the oscillating energy-gap phases. Introduce a genuinely time-dependent Hamiltonian without assuming that exponentiating an instantaneous matrix solves the general problem. The goal is the change of representation; transition approximations and resonant solutions are developed separately.

nodes.label: First-Order Time-Dependent Perturbation Theory
nodes.explanation: Integrate the interaction-picture equation to obtain first-order transition amplitudes caused by a weak finite-duration perturbation. Calculate a pulse-induced transition and the frequency response of a sinusoidal drive, distinguishing amplitudes from probabilities and diagonal phases. Explain the small-transition-probability limit of the approximation. A transition rate into a continuum and nonperturbative Rabi oscillations are separate outcomes.

nodes.label: Rabi Oscillations and the Rotating-Wave Approximation
nodes.explanation: Reduce a sinusoidally driven two-level Hamiltonian to an approximately constant rotating-frame Hamiltonian and calculate resonant and detuned population oscillations. Define drive amplitude, detuning, and the Rabi-frequency convention explicitly. Explain the rotating-wave approximation and when its neglected fast terms matter. Treat coherent population transfer without relaxation; do not confuse this oscillation with a constant golden-rule transition rate.

nodes.label: Density of States for Free Particles
nodes.explanation: Count large-box one-particle levels in wave-vector space and convert the count into the density of states per unit energy. Derive the dimensional dependence using separable box eigenfunctions and interval or spherical-shell volumes, keeping boundary convention and any supplied internal multiplicity explicit. Explain how a dense discrete spectrum becomes a continuum approximation. This is state counting; thermal particle occupancy is outside this lesson.

nodes.label: Fermi's Golden Rule
nodes.explanation: Obtain a transition rate by combining the long-time peak of a perturbative transition probability with the density of final states. Track units and the energy-conservation condition, including absorption or emission from a prescribed harmonic drive. Explain the time window in which a continuum rate is meaningful even though perturbation theory must remain weak. Do not apply a constant rate to an isolated coherently driven pair of levels.

nodes.label: Electric-Dipole Transition Selection Rules
nodes.explanation: Use the prescribed dipole coupling −q E(t)·r to determine which angular-momentum transitions a chosen field polarization can drive. Combine parity with explicit spherical-harmonic matrix elements to derive the orbital Δl and Δm rules, defining the field and polarization components needed. Distinguish a forbidden matrix element from a small radial overlap. Quantization of the electromagnetic field, spontaneous-emission rates, and general tensor-operator theory are excluded.

nodes.label: The Adiabatic Theorem for Isolated Energy Levels
nodes.explanation: Determine when a state follows an instantaneous nondegenerate energy eigenstate as a Hamiltonian changes, including its accumulated dynamical phase. Expand in the instantaneous basis to relate unwanted transitions to parameter-change rates and spectral gaps, using a slowly swept two-level matrix. State smoothness and gap assumptions explicitly and show why a level crossing defeats a naive slowness claim. Geometric phase is reserved for the next enrichment lesson.

nodes.label: Berry Phase in an Adiabatic Cycle
nodes.explanation: Calculate the geometric phase left after removing the dynamical phase from a closed adiabatic parameter cycle. Use a spin in a slowly rotating magnetic field to evaluate the connection and relate the result to the enclosed solid angle, defining the geometry needed. Explain phase-convention changes and how an interference comparison can reveal the phase. Do not introduce non-Abelian holonomy or topological-band invariants.

nodes.label: Addition of Angular Momentum
nodes.explanation: Construct total angular momentum on a tensor-product space and transform between uncoupled and coupled bases. Determine the allowed total j values and calculate the singlet and triplet states of two spins one-half using highest-weight states and lowering operators. Introduce Clebsch–Gordan coefficients through this concrete computation and state the general coupling range. Extensive coefficient tables and general recoupling symbols are outside the lesson.

nodes.label: Spin–Orbit Coupling
nodes.explanation: Use the supplied effective interaction ξ(r)L·S and the identity relating L·S to J², L², and S² to calculate first-order splittings of hydrogenic levels with l greater than zero. Separate the angular eigenvalue from the radial expectation and identify the coupled basis that diagonalizes the perturbation within the Coulomb degeneracy. Explain the model's physical origin without assuming relativistic field theory, and use a fixed nucleus. The l=0 contact contribution and other fine-structure corrections are separate lessons.

nodes.label: The Leading Relativistic Kinetic-Energy Correction
nodes.explanation: Expand the supplied relativistic free-particle energy at low momentum to identify the −p⁴/(8m³c²) perturbation and calculate its hydrogenic first-order energy shift. Introduce the energy-momentum relation and expansion without assuming special-relativity coursework. Use a fixed nucleus and the unperturbed Schrödinger equation to organize expectations, checking that the perturbation is diagonal in the chosen degenerate manifold. Treat this spin-independent term alone; it is not the full fine-structure result.

nodes.label: The Darwin Contact Interaction
nodes.explanation: Apply the supplied effective Darwin interaction for a fixed point Coulomb source and use the delta sampling rule to evaluate its first-order energy shift. Explain why the contact contribution probes the nucleus and acts only on hydrogenic s states, checking its matrix in the degenerate manifold. State that its coefficient is supplied by low-energy relativistic electron theory rather than deriving that theory here. Exclude finite nuclear size, recoil, and radiative corrections.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Fine-Structure Multiplets
nodes.explanation: Combine the kinetic, spin–orbit, and Darwin corrections into the leading hydrogen fine-structure energy and organize the result by n and total j. Show why all three mechanisms are needed, including the special handling of s states, and interpret the splitting of a low-lying manifold. Use a fixed point nucleus and explicitly neglect recoil at this order of treatment. Distinguish fine structure from the Lamb shift and hyperfine structure rather than attempting either calculation.

nodes.label: The Weak-Field Zeeman Effect
nodes.explanation: Calculate magnetic-field splittings of hydrogenic fine-structure levels using the coupled angular-momentum basis and the Landé factor. Derive the needed magnetic-moment expectation from orbital and spin contributions, keeping sign conventions explicit. State that the field is weak compared with the relevant fine-structure separations. Strong-field recoupling, quadratic Zeeman shifts, and hyperfine effects require different approximations and are excluded.

nodes.label: The Linear Stark Effect in Hydrogen
nodes.explanation: Construct and diagonalize the electric-field perturbation within the degenerate n=2 hydrogen manifold. Use parity and the known orbital wavefunctions to identify and evaluate the relevant z matrix element, then interpret the field-selected combinations and linear energy splitting. Define the electrostatic potential-energy sign convention explicitly. Work in the ideal nonrelativistic Coulomb degeneracy; quadratic shifts and competition with fine structure are outside the lesson.

nodes.label: Density Operators and Statistical Mixtures
nodes.explanation: Represent an ensemble by a positive, unit-trace density operator and compute outcome probabilities and expectations using traces. Compare different ensemble decompositions of the same matrix, calculate purity, and evolve the matrix as UρU†. Teach the trace identity needed for these calculations explicitly. Distinguish an incoherent mixture from a coherent superposition; composite-system reduction and environmental decoherence are separate lessons.

nodes.label: Entanglement and Bell States
nodes.explanation: Determine whether a pure two-system state factors and construct the four Bell states in a product basis. Calculate joint and local measurement probabilities in more than one basis to distinguish entangled correlations from a fixed product preparation or a simple classical mixture. Use only finite-dimensional amplitudes and the established phase rules. Quantitative entanglement measures, reduced density matrices, and Bell inequalities follow separately.
nodes.content:
=== SECTION 1: Can one pure state be split into two factors? ===

A joint preparation can have definite correlations even when neither subsystem has a definite local outcome. Are such correlations always described by choosing a separate pure state for each subsystem? The coefficients let us test that question directly.

For two two-dimensional distinguishable systems, use the ordered basis \( |00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle \). A normalized pure state has coefficients \( c_{00},c_{01},c_{10},c_{11} \), with \( \sum_{j,k}|c_{jk}|^2=1 \). It is a product state if there are one-system vectors with coefficients \( a_j \) and \( b_k \) such that \( c_{jk}=a_jb_k \). A pure state that cannot be so factored is entangled.

Put the coefficients into a two-by-two array \( C=\begin{pmatrix}c_{00}&c_{01}\\c_{10}&c_{11}\end{pmatrix} \). For a product,

\[
c_{00}c_{11}-c_{01}c_{10}=a_0b_0a_1b_1-a_0b_1a_1b_0=0.
\]

Conversely, a nonzero two-by-two array with zero determinant has proportional rows, or one zero row. It has rank one and can be written as a column times a row, producing the required coefficients. The nonzero factors can be rescaled into normalized one-system states because the norm of their product is the product of their norms. Thus a normalized pure two-component pair factors exactly when this determinant vanishes.

For example, \( (2,1,2i,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{10} \) factors as \( (1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\otimes(2,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5 \). In contrast, \( (1,0,0,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \) has determinant one-half and cannot factor. The criterion here concerns pure vectors; it is not a test applied to a list of classical preparation probabilities.

[QUESTION 1]
[ANSWER: B]
Which factorization describes the normalized joint column \( (1,i,2,2i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{10} \)?

(A) \( (1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2\otimes(1,2)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5 \)
(B) \( (1,2)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5\otimes(1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \)
(C) \( (1,-2)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5\otimes(1,i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \)
(D) \( (1,2i)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt5\otimes(1,1)^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt2 \)
(E) It cannot factor because its coefficients include imaginary numbers.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: Four Bell states ===

Four useful normalized entangled states are

\[
|\Phi^\pm\rangle=\frac{|00\rangle\pm|11\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad
|\Psi^\pm\rangle=\frac{|01\rangle\pm|10\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
\]

They are called the Bell states. Within each pair the two signs give orthogonal vectors because their overlap is \( (1-1)/2=0 \). States from different pairs have support on disjoint product-basis entries, so those overlaps also vanish. The four vectors form an orthonormal basis of the joint four-dimensional space. Each coefficient array has nonzero determinant, so every one is entangled.

For \( |\Phi^+\rangle \), measuring both subsystems in the original basis gives \( 00 \) or \( 11 \), each with probability one-half. The first subsystem alone has probability one-half for either outcome, found by summing over the second subsystem's possible outcomes. The same is true of the second subsystem. Random local outcomes can coexist with a perfectly definite agreement between their labels.

Introduce a second local basis \( |+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2 \) and \( |-\rangle=(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2 \). Substituting \( |0\rangle=(|+\rangle+|-\rangle)/\sqrt2 \) and \( |1\rangle=(|+\rangle-|-\rangle)/\sqrt2 \) gives

\[
|\Phi^+\rangle=\frac{|++\rangle+|--\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad
|\Phi^-\rangle=\frac{|+-\rangle+|-+\rangle}{\sqrt2},
\]

\[
|\Psi^+\rangle=\frac{|++\rangle-|--\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad
|\Psi^-\rangle=\frac{|-+\rangle-|+-\rangle}{\sqrt2}.
\]

These are changes of representation of each state. The relative sign controls which amplitudes cancel in the second measurement basis.

[TABLE]
Bell state | Joint original-basis outcomes | Joint second-basis outcomes
\( |\Phi^+\rangle \) | Same labels | Same labels
\( |\Phi^-\rangle \) | Same labels | Opposite labels
\( |\Psi^+\rangle \) | Opposite labels | Same labels
\( |\Psi^-\rangle \) | Opposite labels | Opposite labels
[/TABLE]

In each cell there are two allowed pairs, each with probability one-half. Each local marginal is one-half for either outcome in either of these bases. A local marginal means the probability for one subsystem with the other outcome left unconditioned.

[QUESTION 2]
[ANSWER: D]
A preparation is known to be one of the four Bell states. Original-basis measurements always give opposite labels, while measurements in the second local basis always give the same labels. Which preparation is it?

(A) \( |\Phi^+\rangle \)
(B) \( |\Phi^-\rangle \)
(C) \( |\Psi^-\rangle \)
(D) \( |\Psi^+\rangle \)
(E) No Bell state has this pattern.
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: Correlation in one basis is not enough ===

A classical mixture is a preparation procedure that chooses among states with specified probabilities. For example, toss an unrecorded fair coin to prepare \( |00\rangle \) on one result and \( |11\rangle \) on the other. To predict this procedure, calculate each preparation's outcome probability separately and average the probabilities with the coin weights. There is no fixed relative amplitude connecting the two alternatives.

This mixture has the same original-basis probabilities as \( |\Phi^+\rangle \): one-half for \( 00 \), one-half for \( 11 \). But for either product preparation, second-basis measurements give all four pairs with probability one-quarter. Averaging over the coin leaves those four probabilities unchanged. The pure Bell state instead has only \( ++ \) and \( -- \), each with probability one-half. Its relative amplitudes interfere when the measurement basis changes.

For comparison, the fixed product state \( |+\rangle\otimes|+\rangle \) gives four equally likely original-basis pairs but a certain \( ++ \) result in the second basis. The joint distributions distinguish this fixed product preparation, the coin mixture, and the entangled pure preparation. Identical local probabilities in some measurements do not imply identical joint states.

[QUESTION 3]
[ANSWER: A]
Compare the pure state \( |\Phi^-\rangle \) with the fair mixture of \( |00\rangle \) and \( |11\rangle \). Both subsystems are measured in the second basis. Which pair gives the probability of \( ++ \) for the pure state and for the mixture, in that order?

(A) \( 0,1/4 \)
(B) \( 1/2,1/4 \)
(C) \( 1/4,1/4 \)
(D) \( 0,0 \)
(E) \( 1/2,0 \)
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: Local probability and a conditional prediction ===

For any joint pure state, an unconditioned original-basis probability on the first subsystem is \( p_A(j)=\sum_k|c_{jk}|^2 \). A conditional prediction is different: once the first recorded result is known, the joint projector selects only the terms compatible with it and the state is normalized again.

For \( |\Psi^+\rangle \), the first subsystem has unconditioned probability one-half for zero. If a first-subsystem measurement gives zero, the retained joint state is \( |01\rangle \), and the second result is certainly one in the same basis. The original local distribution and the prediction conditioned on a particular readout answer different questions.

[QUESTION 4]
[ANSWER: C]
Prepare \( |\Phi^+\rangle \). The first subsystem is measured in the second basis and gives minus. What are the second subsystem's unconditioned probability of minus before this readout is specified and its conditional probability of minus given that readout?

(A) \( 1,1 \)
(B) \( 1/2,1/2 \)
(C) \( 1/2,1 \)
(D) \( 1/2,0 \)
(E) \( 0,1 \)
[/QUESTION]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: E]
For real \( \theta \), the normalized pure state is \( (|00\rangle+e^{i\theta}|11\rangle)/\sqrt2 \). Which statement holds for the entire family?

(A) It factors whenever \( \theta=0 \).
(B) It factors whenever \( \theta=\pi \).
(C) Its first subsystem has original-basis zero probability \( (1+\cos\theta)/2 \).
(D) It factors for every \( \theta \), because each subsystem has only two basis states.
(E) It is entangled for every \( \theta \), and either local original-basis outcome has probability one-half.
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: The Partial Trace and Reduced Density Operators
nodes.explanation: Calculate a subsystem's reduced density operator by tracing out a finite environment and verify that it reproduces every local measurement probability. Use an entangled pure state to explain how the subsystem can be mixed while the joint system remains pure. Work through basis-index calculations and show that the choice of basis on the discarded system does not affect the result. Do not interpret reduction as a physical collapse of the joint state.

nodes.label: Schmidt Decomposition of Bipartite Pure States
nodes.explanation: Construct a Schmidt decomposition by diagonalizing a reduced density matrix and finding the corresponding partner states. Use Schmidt rank and the shared nonzero reduced eigenvalues to test and quantify pure-state entanglement, introducing the entropy formula and logarithm convention as a consequence. Practise with a two-qubit state. Mixed-state entanglement measures and multipartite canonical forms are outside the lesson.

nodes.label: The CHSH Bell Inequality
nodes.explanation: Derive the CHSH bound for local hidden-variable assignments and calculate a violating spin correlation for an entangled pair with specified measurement axes. State locality and measurement-setting independence explicitly and connect correlation averages to repeated outcomes.
